title: Preoperative classification of histopathological growth patterns in colorectal liver metastases using prospective 18 F-FDG PET/CT.
abstract: Colorectal liver metastases (CLM) exhibit distinct histopathological growth patterns (HGPs) at the metastasis-liver interface, clinically relevant for prognosis and potential predictive value. This study investigates the feasibility of using Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) to preoperatively classify HGPs in CLM and secondly investigate PET parameters as prognostic markers for overall survival (OS). In a prospective study at Umeå University Hospital (June 2013-December 2017), 78 patients with resectable CLM underwent contrast-enhanced liver MRI and 18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging. HGP classification was performed on tissue sections according to 2017 international guidelines. PET features (SUV mean [standardised uptake value], SUV max , metabolic tumour volume [MTV] and first-order texture metrics) were analysed to distinguish encapsulating (eHGP) from replacement (rHGP) patterns. In pretreated patients, multivariate logistic regression including both metabolic and texture parameters identified significant associations for parameters from the fixed level threshold algorithm (VuePoint Sharp IR) with small odds ratios. Overall, PET parameters showed limited ability to discriminate between eHGP and rHGP. OS was superior with eHGP versus rHGP (log-rank p = 0.045). In chemonaïve patients, SUV-based metrics showed unadjusted exploratory associations with OS after liver surgery, varying by reconstruction/delineation and were not significant after correction for multiple testing. FDG-PET-derived parameters were not reliably associated with HGP and did not support non-invasive HGP prediction in this cohort. eHGP was associated with superior survival, underscoring the value of HGP assessment for prognostication while alternative non-invasive biomarkers remain to be identified.

title: Surveillance strategies for the early detection of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors in neurofibromatosis type 1: a systematic review.
abstract: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is the leading cause of cancer-related death in neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), with a lifetime risk of 8-15% and five-year survival below 50% in most series. Imaging surveillance, most often whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WB-MRI), is offered on the premise that earlier detection of premalignant or early malignant lesions permits curative resection, but the supporting evidence has not been formally synthesized. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, we searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane CENTRAL, trial registries, and conference proceedings from 2000 to July 2026 for studies of structured surveillance or lesion characterization in people with NF1. Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently, risk of bias was assessed with design-specific tools, and certainty was graded with GRADE. Sixteen records were included: six surveillance-impact or natural-history cohorts, five imaging diagnostic-accuracy studies, two investigational cell-free DNA studies, and three contextual records (a guideline, a prognostic meta-analysis, and a registered protocol). Because the data were few and heterogeneous, no meta-analysis was possible and the primary objectives could not be addressed quantitatively. The only comparative incidence estimate came from one retrospective cohort compared with expected population-based rates. One retrospective imaging study traced 91% of MPNSTs to a pre-existing distinct nodular lesion. Diffusion-weighted MRI and FDG-PET discriminated benign from malignant tumors with high sensitivity in symptomatic referral cohorts, with threshold-dependent specificity. Harms were inconsistently reported. Certainty was very low for surveillance impact and harms and low for diagnostic accuracy. Current evidence is insufficient to establish whether surveillance improves outcomes; this review informs the design of prospective trials and the next revision of international surveillance guidelines.

title: Baseline OCT Biomarkers Associated with Anatomical Response and Long-Term Reinjection Burden in Diabetic Macular Edema Treated with Intravitreal Dexamethasone Implant.
abstract: Purpose To identify baseline optical coherence tomography (OCT) biomarkers associated with 6 month anatomical response and 36 month reinjection burden in anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF)-pretreated eyes with diabetic macular edema (DME) switched to dexamethasone (DEX) implant. Methods This retrospective single-center cohort included 130 eyes (130 patients) followed for 36 months. Good 6 month anatomical response was defined as a ≥ 20% reduction in central subfield thickness (CST) with complete resolution of intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and frequent reinjection as ≥ 5 DEX implants within 36 months. Multivariable logistic regression was used (Firth penalized regression for reinjection), with a CST-independent fluid-resolution endpoint used as sensitivity analysis. Results Sixty eyes (46.2%) achieved good anatomical response. Hyperreflective foci (HRF; OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.48), disorganization of the retinal inner layers (DRIL; OR 0.16, 0.05-0.47), and external limiting membrane (ELM) disruption (OR 0.16, 0.04-0.54) were independently associated with lower odds of response (optimism-corrected AUC 0.88) and remained significant for fluid resolution. Seventy-nine eyes (60.8%) received ≥ 5 implants. Ellipsoid zone (EZ) disruption (OR 24.83, 3.73-345.08) and DRIL (OR 5.03, 1.45-20.27) were independently associated with frequent reinjection (optimism-corrected AUC 0.95). Month-6 and month-36 anatomical status agreed in 85.4% of eyes. Intraocular pressure > 25 mmHg occurred in 26.2% of eyes, all controlled medically. Conclusion Baseline OCT biomarkers were associated with both early anatomical response and long-term reinjection burden after switching to DEX. HRF, DRIL, and ELM disruption were associated with a lower likelihood of 6 month response, whereas EZ disruption and DRIL were associated with a higher 36 month reinjection burden. These prognostic associations require external validation.

Ellipsoid zone (EZ) disruption (OR 24.83, 3.73-345.08) and DRIL (OR 5.03, 1.45-20.27) were independently associated with frequent reinjection (optimism-corrected AUC 0.95). Month-6 and month-36 anatomical status agreed in 85.4% of eyes. Intraocular pressure > 25 mmHg occurred in 26.2% of eyes, all controlled medically.

Baseline OCT biomarkers were associated with both early anatomical response and long-term reinjection burden after switching to DEX. title: Retinal oxidative, structural and functional outcomes following melatonin administration in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats.
abstract: Purpose To characterize additional retinal oxidative, structural and functional outcomes in a previously published cohort of streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats.-- Street E 42, Redenção, Vitória de Santo Antão, PE, 55,612-050, Brazil. - methods Fifty male Wistar rats were allocated to control, untreated diabetic, concurrent melatonin, delayed melatonin or insulin-treated groups (10 per group). Melatonin was administered subcutaneously at 10 mg/kg for 20 days, starting at diabetes induction or after confirmation. Retinal superoxide production, NADPH oxidase activity, histology and microvascular morphology were assessed. Morphometry used five slides from five animals per group (one slide per animal; n = 5). Pancreatic glutathione and lipid peroxidation were additional tissue-specific measures. Electroretinography was described qualitatively because numerical results were unavailable. Previously published glycemic and insulin results are not reproduced. Results Both melatonin groups showed lower retinal oxidative measures and more favorable morphometric outcomes than untreated diabetic animals. The reported comparisons did not identify significant differences between melatonin schedules for these endpoints. Pancreatic oxidative measures were also more favorable in treated animals. Descriptive electrophysiological observations did not establish functional recovery. Conclusion These findings extend the oxidative and morphological characterization of melatonin-associated retinal changes in a shared cohort. Neither schedule showed clear superiority and functional benefits or reversal of established retinopathy remain unproven.

title: Outcomes of cataract surgery in eyes with chorio-retinal coloboma.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the visual outcomes and complications of cataract surgery in eyes with chorio-retinal coloboma. Methods Retrospective review of patients with coloboma who underwent cataract surgery between 2015 and 2024 was done. Complications and postoperative visual acuity were assessed. The association of visual outcomes with factors such as preoperative age, best corrected visual acuity, disc/macular involvement, presence of nystagmus, strabismus, cataract grade, type of surgery, intra and postoperative complications and intraocular lens implantation status was analyzed. Result 556 eyes of 496 patients with coloboma who underwent cataract extraction were included. Postoperative visual acuity improved significantly compared with preoperative visual acuity (median of logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution: 1.4 vs. 0.8; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Z = - 17.76, p < 0.001, r = 0.78). Post-operative visual outcomes are associated with preoperative best corrected visual acuity, disc/macular involvement, presence of nystagmus, age and aphakia status. Intraoperative complications were posterior capsular rupture in 63 (15.5%) eyes, descemets membrane detachment in 4 eyes (0.9%). Second surgical interventions included endothelial keratoplasty for corneal decompensation in 5 (0.89%) cases, intraocular lens (IOL) explantation for significant IOL decentration in 14 (2.51%) eyes and vitreoretinal surgery for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in 31 (5.57%) cases. Conclusion Cataract surgery was associated with a significant improvement in visual acuity in eyes with coloboma. However, visual outcomes may be suboptimal due to pre-existing posterior segment colobomatous involvement and presence of nystagmus. Preoperative planning, and a tailored surgical approach are essential for cataract surgery in coloboma eyes.

title: Predicting OCT-derived retinal and choroidal thickness phenotypes in adults with diabetes using a tabular foundation model integrating ocular biometry and systemic health data.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate whether systemic health data and ocular biometry can predict distribution-defined central macular thickness (CMT) and subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT) phenotypes in adults with diabetes using a tabular foundation model. Methods We analyzed Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data (2017-2021). Upper- and lower-tail CMT and SFCT phenotypes were defined using 3%, 5%, and 10% cutoffs from the 2017-2019 development cohort and evaluated in the independent 2020-2021 temporal validation cohort. Systemic-only and anatomy-aware models, incorporating axial length and anterior chamber depth, were compared. Participant-grouped cross-validation prevented fellow-eye leakage. Discrimination, calibration, and incremental performance were assessed. Results Overall, Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a tabular foundation model, demonstrated stronger predictive performance than conventional machine-learning algorithms across most phenotype prediction tasks. The CMT and SFCT cohorts comprised 3,732 and 3,699 eyes, respectively. In temporal validation, anatomy-aware TabPFN achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.722 (high CMT 3%), 0.745 (low CMT 3%), 0.817 (high SFCT 3%), and 0.880 (low SFCT 3%). Adding ocular biometry significantly improved prediction of low SFCT phenotypes compared with systemic-only TabPFN (ΔAUC, 0.121-0.157; all P ≤ 0.003), but not compared with age-plus-axial-length logistic regression. Positive predictive values were low for rare phenotypes, and calibration varied across tasks. Conclusions Anatomy-aware TabPFN predicted extreme OCT thickness phenotypes, particularly low SFCT, but much of the gain may reflect established axial-length-related anatomy. Clinical utility for OCT triage remains unproven and requires external validation.

title: Whole-Brain Dynamics and Cognitive Flexibility in Level 1 ASD: An HMM-Based Approach.
abstract: Purpose Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by differences in cognitive flexibility, which are closely associated with restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). However, the dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural correlates of cognitive flexibility difficulties in ASD by analyzing dynamic brain network features and explored their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. Methods We applied hidden Markov models (HMMs) to resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to characterize dynamic brain network states in children with ASD (n = 69) and typically developing (TD) children (n = 50). Cognitive flexibility was assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF). An independent ABIDE II dataset was used for external validation. Machine learning models evaluated the diagnostic utility of behavioral and neuroimaging markers. Results Children with ASD showed atypical brain network dynamics, specifically a reduced brain state switching rate (p < 0.01) and asymmetric activation of the frontoparietal network (FPN). These alterations were significantly associated with cognitive flexibility difficulties and RRB severity in the ASD group (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q < 0.05) and generalized to the independent sample. Combining cognitive flexibility scores with brain state switching rates yielded high diagnostic accuracy (internal AUC: 0.897 (95% CI 0.812-0.963); external AUC: 0.869 (95% CI 0.781-0.943)). Conclusion This study provides novel insights into the dynamic neural mechanisms underlying cognitive flexibility differences in ASD. The findings support combined behavioral and neuroimaging biomarkers for improving ASD diagnosis and lay the groundwork for individualized intervention research.

title: Bridging Gaps in Cancer Screening Knowledge: Impact of Community-Based Education Among High-Risk Populations in the Synergistic Partnership for Enhancing Excellence in Cancer Health (SPEECH) Program.
abstract: Community-based education may reduce disparities in breast and colorectal cancer (BC/CRC) screening, particularly among individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) and lower educational attainment. We evaluated whether the Synergistic Partnership for Enhancing Excellence in Cancer Health (SPEECH) BC/CRC education program improved knowledge of screening recommendations and whether gains differed across participant subgroups in the U54 Community Outreach Core (COC) cohort serving high-risk and under-resourced communities. Among 453 participants (median age, 57.7 years; 69.3% female), 41.7% had LEP and 33.6% had less than a high school education. Insurance and primary care access were high (86.3% and 85.2%), yet screening rates remained modest (CRC, 42.4%; mammography, 54.2%). Among 395 participants with matched pre/post surveys, knowledge improved significantly after SPEECH education (all p < 0.0001): correct CRC screening age increased from 38.7% to 83.3%, mammography screening age from 40.3% to 69.6%, and TP53 knowledge from 56.2% to 89.9%. High composite knowledge scores increased from 39.0% to 89.6%. Knowledge gains differed significantly across education levels for CRC, TP53, and total knowledge. Participants with LEP demonstrated greater gains in knowledge than those without LEP. A brief community education program substantially improved cancer screening knowledge, particularly among participants facing educational and language barriers. Despite high healthcare access, screening remained suboptimal. Pairing education with patient navigation and longitudinal follow-up may help translate knowledge gains into improved screening participation and clarify whether it can lead changes in screening behavior.

title: Mapping Research on AI-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support Systems: a Bibliometric Study Integrating Google Trends and Content Analysis.
abstract: Background Research on artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis and clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) is expanding, but integrated evidence on publication patterns, keyword trajectories, online search activity, and methodological characteristics remains limited. Objective To characterize AI-CDSS research by integrating bibliometric analysis, Google Trends comparison, and structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications. Methods Scholarly interest was assessed using bibliometric analysis of Web of Science records from 2016 through August 2026, including author-keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and reference co-citation, whereas Google Trends was used to characterize online search activity. A structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications was conducted to examine applications, methodological characteristics, and reported limitations. Results We analyzed 19,809 included publications from 2016 through August 2026. Output rose approximately 21-fold, from 193 records in 2016 to 4,082 in 2025. Output was geographically concentrated within the included corpus, with a Gini coefficient of 0.869. Among records with identifiable corresponding-author country or territory, China, the United States, and India accounted for 61.33%. Scientific Reports was the most frequent source (n = 916). Frequent artificial intelligence- and diagnosis-related keywords included machine learning (n = 5,666), deep learning (n = 4,022), and computer-aided diagnosis (n = 1,512). Bibliographic coupling identified 15 publication communities, and reference co-citation identified seven reference communities. In the monthly level-series comparison, 9 of 10 keyword concepts exhibited significant associations with Google Trends relative search interest, but none of the 10 first-difference associations remained significant after Bonferroni adjustment. Content analysis of 215 citation-ranked publications, including 191 empirical publications, showed frequent use of convolutional neural networks in diagnostic and radiology applications. Common limitations included limited external validation, infrequent calibration reporting, and sparse workflow-level or impact evaluation. Conclusion AI-CDSS research has rapidly expanded around machine learning, deep learning, and diagnostic applications, but the analyzed citation-ranked publications provide more evidence of methodological development than of clinical deployment. Integrating bibliometric, search-activity, and content-based perspectives shows limited short-term correspondence between online search activity and scholarly keyword use and highlights the need to move beyond model development toward independent external validation, prospective workflow and patient-outcome evaluation, calibration, fairness, and postdeployment monitoring.

title: Mapping the AI-Enabled Medical Device Landscape in Australia and the United States: a Comparative Analysis of FDA and TGA Listings.
abstract: This cross-sectional descriptive study mapped the AI-enabled medical device landscape in Australia and the United States using the FDA AI/ML-enabled medical device list and the TGA AI-enabled medical devices list, current as of 5th January 2026. We compared medical specialty distribution, AI function, regulatory risk classification, and manufacturer origin, and characterised the overlap between the two lists. We identified 1,357 FDA listings and 125 TGA listings. Radiology dominated both markets (FDA 76.5%, TGA 60.8%), but Australia had different specialty diversity to the US, including orthopaedic (2.4%) and dental (3.2%) devices. AI image and signal interpretation was most common (FDA 57.5%, TGA 38.4%), whereas measurement, treatment planning, and workflow support were relatively more prominent in Australia. Nearly all FDA devices were Class II (98.8%), while TGA devices spanned low to high-risk classes. Top contributors to Australia's AI market were the USA (28.8%), Australia (9.6%), and China (8.8%). Of the 125 TGA listings, 71 (56.8%) had a matching FDA listing. Among these 71 matched TGA listings, 15 were listed in Australia prior to the USA, while the remaining 56 were FDA-listed first. Australia's AI device market is smaller, but still diverse, and includes multiple Australian-headquartered manufacturers. The substantial overlap between the two lists, predominantly with prior FDA listing, suggests the Australian market draws on internationally developed technologies, although listing dates do not establish when devices became available to clinicians. These descriptive findings provide a benchmark for future comparative and longitudinal research as both markets continue to develop.

title: Explainable machine learning predictive models for treatment response after SBRT in melanoma brain metastases.
abstract: Purpose/objective To develop an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model to predict the complete/partial response of oligometastatic brain lesions from melanoma (MBMs) two months after from radiosurgical or fractionated stereotactic treatments. Material/methods 50 consecutive patients with a total 102 MBMs treated with CyberKnife® SBRT from December 2012 to December 2018 were selected within the Rabbit study. Local response was evaluated on brain MRI performed during follow-up using response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (RECIST) and revised using response criteria for brain metastases from the response assessment in neuro-oncology criteria (RANO) group. For each treated lesion, the following variables were considered: number of treated lesions, the LDH pre-treatment level, previous treatments (surgery or whole brain RT), BRAF status, time from primary diagnosis to brain lesions discovery (Time_diag), lesion dimensions and site, SBRT dose and fractionation, type of concomitant treatment with ipilimumab (IPI). Six different supervised machine learning models, including logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), decision tree (DT) and light gradient boosting (LGBM), were trained and internally validated with 5-fold cross validation. Model performances were assessed using receiving operator curves (ROC) and area under the curve (AUC). An explainable approach based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was deployed to generate individual explanations of the model decisions. Lastly, a decision tree was created to better understand and interpret the complex relationships between the covariates and the target variable. Results 23.5% of lesions had a complete or partial response and were used as ground truth for the ML models. The best performing model was the LGBM, reporting a mean AUCs in the 5-fold cross validation of 0.87 (0.85-0.91). SHAP analysis strongly associated complete/partial response with four variables, namely in order of importance: the BRAF status, the total dose, the type of treatment with ipilimumab, and the lesion dimension. In particular, the DT classified patients with BRAF "wild-type" status having only 10.7% probability to reach complete/partial response. Among these lesions, those treated with doses < 24 Gy had 0% probability of complete/partial response. By contrast, lesions with a BRAF "mutated" status reported a probability of complete/partial response of 39.1%. title: Lateral and suprasellar MRI anatomy in pituitary neuroendocrine tumor surgery: interobserver agreement and associations with resection and intraoperative CSF leakage.
abstract: Purpose Lateral cavernous-sinus extension and suprasellar tumor-arachnoid anatomy are distinct but overlapping dimensions of pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET) surgery. We evaluated whether reader-concordant preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) descriptors of these two axes show different associations with extent of resection and intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. Methods In this single-center retrospective study, two blinded neurosurgeons independently assessed preoperative MRI of 53 patients: modified Knosp grade, suprasellar height, bowing index, infundibular deviation angle, and a study-specific tumor-arachnoid cleft grade. Exploratory analyses examined resection extent and Esposito-graded leakage (15 events), with post hoc adjustment for maximal tumor diameter. Results Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were 0.995-0.999 for continuous measures; cleft agreement was 53/53 and Knosp exact agreement 96.2%. Knosp grade was most strongly associated with non-total resection (area under the curve [AUC] 0.908; diameter-adjusted odds ratio [OR] 10.8 per SD, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.4-48.9) but not leakage (AUC 0.648). Suprasellar height (AUC 0.747) and cleft grade (AUC 0.740) showed stronger leakage associations; none of 16 patients with a wide cleft (> 2 mm) leaked. Cleft grade and height were strongly collinear (ρ=-0.81); the cleft-leakage association persisted after diameter adjustment (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.19-0.93). Conclusion Lateral and suprasellar MRI descriptors, concordant between two readers, showed different, partly overlapping operative associations. Modified Knosp grade related most strongly to resection, whereas suprasellar features, particularly the study-specific cleft grade, showed stronger exploratory associations with intraoperative leakage. The cleft finding is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective external validation; added value over height and the sellar barrier is unproven.

title: Diffusion anisotropy as an imaging biomarker of directional progression in temporal glioblastoma.
abstract: Purpose Glioblastoma frequently progresses beyond surgical margins, yet whether preoperative imaging can predict its direction remains unclear. Given the anatomical characteristics of the temporal lobe and the potential role of anterior temporal lobectomy, we evaluated FLAIR, isotropic diffusion (DTI-p), and diffusion anisotropy (DTI-q) as imaging biomarkers of directional progression after complete resection. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively recruited multicenter cohort of patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma confined to the temporal lobe who underwent complete resection of contrast-enhancing tumor and had preoperative diffusion tensor imaging and follow-up MRI demonstrating progression. Progression was visually classified relative to the resection cavity. Direction-specific accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were calculated, with paired comparisons using exact McNemar tests and Holm correction across all comparisons. Times to progression and death were summarized descriptively. Results Thirty-two patients met inclusion criteria. DTI-q demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy across all progression directions (median, 75%), compared with DTI-p (median, 50%) and FLAIR (median, 44%). DTI-q significantly outperformed FLAIR and DTI-p for lateral, superior, and inferior progression after Holm correction. Combined imaging models did not improve predictive performance over DTI-q alone. Conclusion Preoperative DTI-q predicted directional progression after complete resection more accurately than FLAIR or DTI-p, supporting DTI-q as a potential imaging biomarker for spatially informed surgical planning.

title: Predicting long-term tumor response to Gamma Knife radiosurgery in vestibular schwannoma: an integrated model of auto-segmentation, MRI radiomics, and dosimetric parameters.
abstract: Aims Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is a common benign intracranial tumor for which Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) is an important treatment option. However, post-treatment changes in tumor volume vary considerably and can complicate follow-up and response assessment. This study developed a framework that uses deep learning-based segmentation and MRI radiomics to predict long-term treatment response to GKRS for VS. Methods We developed an nnU-Net model to automate VS segmentation on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI. Patients with long-term follow-up after GKRS were classified into four response patterns: direct regression, delayed regression, stable disease, and growth. A two-stage machine-learning framework was then constructed. Stage 1 distinguishes regression from non-regression, while Stage 2 differentiates direct from delayed regression. Pretreatment MRI radiomics features were combined with clinical and dose-related variables and used to train multiple machine-learning models. The models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret the results. Results The nnU-Net model achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 91.16 ± 0.47% on the external test dataset. Among the 155 patients, 53 showed direct regression, 83 delayed regression, 9 stable disease, and 10 tumor growths. In Stage 1, the Balanced Random Forest algorithm achieved accuracy of 74.19 ± 7.21%, an AUROC of 72.43 ± 10.18%, and AUPRC of 93.08 ± 4.27%. In Stage 2, the Support Vector Machine achieved accuracy of 64.05 ± 4.16%, an AUROC of 66.70 ± 6.21%, and AUPRC of 57.10 ± 7.30%. SHAP analysis identified radiomics and dose-related features as important predictors. Conclusion Deep learning-based segmentation combined with pretreatment MRI radiomics, clinical variables, and dose-related parameters may provide useful information for predicting long-term response after GKRS for VS. This framework could support more individualized follow-up planning and help clinicians distinguish delayed regression from treatment failure.

title: Hypoxia-powered MRI guides supramaximal biosurgical sampling of glioblastoma infiltration: the GLIOXY initiative.
abstract: Purpose To assess the feasibility of using hypoxia-powered magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to guide prospective sampling of high-response habitats beyond contrast enhancement in glioblastoma. Methods Nine treatment-naive patients with histologically confirmed isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wildtype glioblastoma underwent blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) MRI during a controlled transient hypoxic stimulus on the evening before surgery. Anatomical segmentation and voxel-wise temporal decomposition generated normalized hypoxia response maps. Otsu thresholding defined a high-response habitat outside contrast enhancement. Targets were confirmed with the surgeon according to anatomical accessibility and eloquence, transferred to neuronavigation, and sampled before major debulking. We divided the specimen for formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded neuropathology and frozen-tissue storage. Results Neuronavigation transfer succeeded in all nine cases. Eight targets were accessible and sampled. Seven sampled targets contained tumor. One yielded reactive cortex and white matter without definite tumor. No target-sampling complications were observed among the eight sampled procedures. Conclusion Hypoxia-powered MRI could be integrated into prospective neuronavigation-guided sampling beyond contrast enhancement. Tumor was identified in seven of eight sampled targets. By translating a tracer-free physiological response map into coordinate-matched tissue, the GLIOXY workflow enables prospective, targeted tissue sampling of non-enhancing glioblastoma regions.

title: Serial serum lactate dehydrogenase dynamics as an adjunctive biomarker for differentiating true progression from treatment-related changes in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma.
abstract: Background Differentiating true tumor progression from pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis remains a major clinical challenge in patients with IDH-wild-type glioblastoma after radiotherapy and temozolomide. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is inexpensive, widely available and repeatable, but it is a nonspecific systemic marker whose tissue source cannot be inferred from total serum activity. We therefore evaluated serial LDH dynamics as an adjunctive, hypothesis-generating biomarker rather than as a glioblastoma-specific tumor marker. Methods We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients treated at a single tertiary neuro-oncology center with histologically confirmed IDH-wild-type glioblastoma who developed new or increasing contrast enhancement after standard radiochemotherapy and had available serum LDH measurements at baseline and at the time of suspicious MRI. Final diagnosis was assigned using histology when available or a composite reference standard based on multidisciplinary review and longitudinal imaging follow-up. LDH at suspicious MRI and LDH percentage change from baseline were evaluated for their ability to distinguish true progression from treatment-related changes. Results The cohort included 180 patients: 101 with true progression and 79 with treatment-related changes, including 65 pseudoprogression and 14 radiation necrosis cases. Median LDH at suspicious MRI was higher in true progression than in treatment-related changes (371 vs 273 U/L), as was median LDH percentage increase from baseline (28.7% vs 5.8%). Baseline LDH showed limited discrimination (AUC 0.675), whereas event LDH and LDH percentage change showed stronger performance (AUC 0.855 and 0.872, respectively). An exploratory LDH signature, defined as event LDH ≥ 293 U/L or LDH increase ≥ 25%, showed high sensitivity (95.0%) and negative predictive value (90.0%) but moderate specificity (57.0%). Conclusions In this single-center retrospective cohort, serial total-serum LDH dynamics were associated with final diagnostic classification after suspicious post-treatment MRI in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma. Because serum LDH is biologically nonspecific and the present study did not determine LDH isoenzymes or cellular origin, LDH should not be interpreted as a glioma-specific tumor marker or used as a stand-alone test. Its potential role is limited to an adjunctive signal within a multimodal RANO-informed diagnostic framework, and prospective external validation with source-resolved LDH analyses is required.

Differentiating true tumor progression from pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis remains a major clinical challenge in patients with IDH-wild-type glioblastoma after radiotherapy and temozolomide. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is inexpensive, widely available and repeatable, but it is a nonspecific systemic marker whose tissue source cannot be inferred from total serum activity. We therefore evaluated serial LDH dynamics as an adjunctive, hypothesis-generating biomarker rather than as a glioblastoma-specific tumor marker.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients treated at a single tertiary neuro-oncology center with histologically confirmed IDH-wild-type glioblastoma who developed new or increasing contrast enhancement after standard radiochemotherapy and had available serum LDH measurements at baseline and at the time of suspicious MRI. Final diagnosis was assigned using histology when available or a composite reference standard based on multidisciplinary review and longitudinal imaging follow-up. LDH at suspicious MRI and LDH percentage change from baseline were evaluated for their ability to distinguish true progression from treatment-related changes.

Results

The cohort included 180 patients: 101 with true progression and 79 with treatment-related changes, including 65 pseudoprogression and 14 radiation necrosis cases. Median LDH at suspicious MRI was higher in true progression than in treatment-related changes (371 vs 273 U/L), as was median LDH percentage increase from baseline (28.7% vs 5.8%). Baseline LDH showed limited discrimination (AUC 0.675), whereas event LDH and LDH percentage change showed stronger performance (AUC 0.855 and 0.872, respectively). An exploratory LDH signature, defined as event LDH ≥ 293 U/L or LDH increase ≥ 25%, showed high sensitivity (95.0%) and negative predictive value (90.0%) but moderate specificity (57.0%).

Conclusions

In this single-center retrospective cohort, serial total-serum LDH dynamics were associated with final diagnostic classification after suspicious post-treatment MRI in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma. Because serum LDH is biologically nonspecific and the present study did not determine LDH isoenzymes or cellular origin, LDH should not be interpreted as a glioma-specific tumor marker or used as a stand-alone test. Its potential role is limited to an adjunctive signal within a multimodal RANO-informed diagnostic framework, and prospective external validation with source-resolved LDH analyses is required.

title: MRI-defined necrosis morphology, circulating immune profiles and survival in glioblastoma.
abstract: Purpose Necrosis is a defining feature and an active hypoxic niche implicated in immune escape and treatment resistance in glioblastoma (GBM). We asked whether MRI-defined necrosis morphology is associated with circulating immune profiles and overall survival (OS). Methods We retrospectively studied 111 patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype GBM resected in 2018-2024. Preoperative necrosis was classified visually as classic confluent or multiloculated. Two blinded readers reclassified all cases independently. Immune subsets were assessed by flow cytometry (n = 59, 48/11 classic/multiloculated) and plasma cytokines by multiplex immunoassay (n = 54, 45/9). All 28 immune analytes were exploratory, corrected across the panel. OS from surgery was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier and Cox models, including treatment and small-sample sensitivity analyses. Results Inter-reader agreement was kappa = 0.883. Multiloculated morphology was associated with longer OS (median, 17.4 vs. 14.4 months; HR, 0.55, 95% CI, 0.31-0.98, p = 0.041), including after multivariable adjustment (n = 94; HR, 0.42, 0.22-0.81, p = 0.010; Firth-penalized, 0.44, p = 0.007), exclusion of untreated patients and early deaths, and restriction to completed chemoradiation (HR, 0.37, 0.16-0.84, p = 0.018). Classic morphology was associated with fewer conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) (0.15% vs. 0.41%, p = 0.006), more mature natural killer cells (p = 0.022), and lower granzyme B, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, and IL-10, but no difference survived correction (lowest q = 0.088). Multiloculated patients were younger (57.2 vs. 64.3 years, p = 0.032). The cDC association did not persist after adjustment for deep-seated location (p = 0.124). Conclusions Multiloculated necrosis was associated with longer OS after adjustment for established prognostic factors, which requires external validation. Circulating immune differences were exploratory and could not be separated from tumor location. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Preoperative tumor burden predicts recurrence-free survival in WHO grade 2 meningiomas: a multivariable survival analysis.
abstract: Purpose Recurrence remains a major concern following resection of World Health Organization (WHO) grade 2 meningiomas. Identification of preoperative factors associated with recurrence may improve risk stratification and inform postoperative surveillance and treatment strategies. We sought to identify clinical and radiographic predictors of recurrence-free survival (RFS) in patients with WHO grade 2 meningiomas. Methods We retrospectively analyzed adults undergoing resection of intracranial WHO grade 2 meningiomas from 2010 to 2023. Clinical, radiographic, surgical, and treatment-related variables were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression. Preoperative tumor burden was estimated volumetrically using an ellipsoid-based method. The multivariable model included preoperative tumor volume, Simpson grade, skull base location, and planned adjuvant radiotherapy (RT). Alternative measures of surgical outcome were assessed in sensitivity analyses. Results Among 136 surgical episodes, 38 recurrences occurred. Median preoperative tumor volume was 28.5 cm³. On univariable analysis, greater preoperative tumor volume was associated with worse RFS (HR 1.52, 95% CI 1.11-2.10; p = 0.010) and remained independently associated with RFS after multivariable adjustment (HR 1.47, 95% CI 1.05-2.05; p = 0.024). Recurrence occurred in 15.6%, 23.9%, and 44.4% of small-, intermediate-, and large-volume tertiles, respectively (log-rank p = 0.0048). Simpson grade showed a borderline association with RFS, while skull base location and planned RT were not independently associated with RFS. Conclusions Among evaluated clinical, radiographic, and treatment-related factors, preoperative tumor burden emerged as an independent predictor of RFS in WHO grade 2 meningiomas. Preoperative volumetric assessment may provide a readily available imaging marker to improve recurrence risk stratification.

title: Application of augmented reality in frame-based stereotactic brain biopsy: a case series feasibility study.
abstract: Purpose Frame-based stereotactic biopsy (STB) lacks intraoperative visual control. Augmented reality (AR) via Microsoft HoloLens 2 offers real-time visualization of the biopsy needle. This study evaluates the technical feasibility and preliminary clinical results of AR navigation during standard frame-based STB. Methods This prospective single-center pilot study included 10 adults undergoing STB for intracranial lesions. Standard trajectory planning utilized the Cosman-Roberts-Wells (CRW ® ) stereotactic frame, intraoperative computed tomography (CT), and preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in NeuroSight Arc ® . Concurrently, Medgital software and HoloLens 2 displayed a hologram of the patient's head, lesion, and trajectory. A passive tracker on the biopsy needle enabled real-time holographic visualization. Endpoints included technical feasibility, registration time, navigation error, diagnostic yield, and complications. Results AR navigation feasibility was confirmed in all 10 patients (100%). Mean registration time was 79 ± 27 s, and mean AR trajectory error relative to standard planning was 2.21 ± 0.67 mm. A definitive histological diagnosis was obtained in all 10 cases (mean passes: 2.4). No hemorrhagic complications or mortality occurred. Conclusion Integrating AR navigation (HoloLens 2 and Medgital) with conventional frame-based STB is potentially technically feasible, safe, fast, and provides acceptable accuracy. AR complements the standard workflow by offering direct intraoperative visualization of the needle trajectory.

title: A novel spherical applicator for ultrasound-guided assessment of tumor resection in intracranial surgery.
abstract: Purpose Intraoperative ultrasound (iUS) provides real-time imaging during brain tumor resection, but its utility may be limited by surgical cavity collapse and distortion of surrounding anatomy. We developed a spherical ultrasound applicator intended to provide a reproducible imaging interface within the resection cavity, with the potential to support cavity geometry during post-resection assessment. This study evaluated the feasibility of applicator placement and ultrasound image acquisition across simulated resection cavity geometries and imaging conditions. Methods A spherical applicator with a 17.5-mm radius and central ultrasound probe channel was fabricated and evaluated using silicone phantoms representing shallow, deep, and irregular resection cavities. Ultrasound imaging was performed using phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and 1% albumin as acoustic coupling media. Embedded echogenic targets at depths of approximately 3 and 5 cm were evaluated using contrast-to-noise ratios (CNR). Computed tomography was used to verify phantom geometry and applicator fit. Results The applicator maintained stable contact with simulated cavity surfaces and enabled visualization of cavity margins across all three phantom geometries. Echogenic targets remained detectable at depths up to 5 cm using either coupling medium. At 3 cm, CNR values were 11.88 with PBS and 11.37 with albumin, decreasing to 6.76 and 6.24, respectively, at 5 cm. Imaging depth, rather than coupling medium, was the predominant determinant of target contrast. Computed tomography confirmed phantom geometry and applicator alignment. Conclusion This phantom-based feasibility study demonstrates that a spherical ultrasound applicator can provide a reproducible acoustic interface for imaging simulated brain tumor resection cavities. The device may facilitate intraoperative assessment of cavity margins and potentially complement intracavitary radiation delivery. Further in vivo evaluation is required to establish clinical utility.

title: Molecular Imaging of Liver Fibrosis using [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT: A Prospective head-to-head comparison with Transient Elastography, Serum Biomarkers & Metavir Histopathological Staging.
abstract: Chronic liver disease (CLD) leading to cirrhosis is a major cause of global morbidity and mortality. Histopathological evaluation by liver biopsy remains the gold standard for fibrosis staging, but its invasive nature limits routine use. Non-invasive tools such as serum biomarkers and transient elastography (TE) are widely used but they have recognised limitations. This prospective study performed a comprehensive head-to-head comparison of [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT uptake with serum fibrosis scores, TE, and histopathology across all stages of liver fibrosis in a well-characterised CLD cohort. Materials and methods Fifty-four patients with CLD of different etiologies (51.9% non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [NAFLD], 29.6% viral hepatitis, 11.1% autoimmune hepatitis) underwent [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT together with clinical and biochemical evaluation. Serum fibrosis markers (APRI, FIB-4, and NFS) were calculated, and TE was performed in 52 patients. Liver biopsy (n = 22) was obtained when clinically indicated, or in cases of discordance between non-invasive tests. Hepatic tracer uptake was quantified employing two methodologies (a) a four-region-of-interest (4-ROI) approach as well as (b) whole-liver segmentation approach. Correlations between FAPI uptake and fibrosis markers were assessed using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis determined diagnostic performance for clinically significant fibrosis (≥ F2) and cirrhosis (F4). Patients with discrepant results underwent systematic re-evaluation with repeat TE and/or histopathology to establish a conclusive diagnosis. Additionally, an agreement analysis between the 4-ROI method and whole-liver segmentation was assessed for background-corrected SUVmean using Bland-Altman analysis. The strength of agreement was quantified using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). Results Hepatic [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 uptake increased progressively with advancing fibrosis, being visually evident in advanced stages (F3-F4) and rising in parallel with liver stiffness measurement (LSM). Uptake correlated moderately with LSM, APRI, and FIB-4. For clinically significant fibrosis (≥ F2), an average SUVmean threshold (4-ROI) of 0.76 yielded 86.0% sensitivity and 88.9% specificity (AUC 0.88). For cirrhosis (F4), an average SUVmax threshold of 3.13 provided 90.9% specificity (AUC 0.79). The simplified 4-ROI method showed excellent agreement with whole-liver segmentation for background-corrected SUVmean (ICC 0.96, Lin's CCC 0.95, no significant proportional bias) and statistically equivalent diagnostic performance (DeLong p ≥ 0.33). Among discrepant cases, molecular imaging correctly reclassified the majority of patients in whom elastography and FAPI PET disagreed, which was confirmed by repeat TE or biopsy. Conclusion This prospective study provides evidence that [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT is a reliable non-invasive biomarker of hepatic stellate cell activation, that outperforms conventional methods in clinically discrepant cases of liver fibrosis, while offering whole-liver imaging that is less affected by common confounders. It reliably excludes advanced fibrosis and may help avoid unnecessary liver biopsy. These findings position FAPI PET as a problem-solving tool in CLD management.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis determined diagnostic performance for clinically significant fibrosis (≥ F2) and cirrhosis (F4). Patients with discrepant results underwent systematic re-evaluation with repeat TE and/or histopathology to establish a conclusive diagnosis. Additionally, an agreement analysis between the 4-ROI method and whole-liver segmentation was assessed for background-corrected SUVmean using Bland-Altman analysis. The strength of agreement was quantified using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC).

Results

Hepatic [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 uptake increased progressively with advancing fibrosis, being visually evident in advanced stages (F3-F4) and rising in parallel with liver stiffness measurement (LSM). Uptake correlated moderately with LSM, APRI, and FIB-4. For clinically significant fibrosis (≥ F2), an average SUVmean threshold (4-ROI) of 0.76 yielded 86.0% sensitivity and 88.9% specificity (AUC 0.88). For cirrhosis (F4), an average SUVmax threshold of 3.13 provided 90.9% specificity (AUC 0.79). The simplified 4-ROI method showed excellent agreement with whole-liver segmentation for background-corrected SUVmean (ICC 0.96, Lin's CCC 0.95, no significant proportional bias) and statistically equivalent diagnostic performance (DeLong p ≥ 0.33). Among discrepant cases, molecular imaging correctly reclassified the majority of patients in whom elastography and FAPI PET disagreed, which was confirmed by repeat TE or biopsy.

Conclusion

This prospective study provides evidence that [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT is a reliable non-invasive biomarker of hepatic stellate cell activation, that outperforms conventional methods in clinically discrepant cases of liver fibrosis, while offering whole-liver imaging that is less affected by common confounders. It reliably excludes advanced fibrosis and may help avoid unnecessary liver biopsy. These findings position FAPI PET as a problem-solving tool in CLD management.

title: The Changing Metastatic Landscape in the Modern Oncologic Era: Emerging Tumor Behaviors, Procedure-Related Dissemination, and Implications for [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT Interpretation: A Structured Narrative Review.
abstract: Background Classical metastatic patterns, rooted in Paget's seed-and-soil hypothesis, have guided oncologic imaging interpretation for over a century. The widespread adoption of immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and minimally invasive surgical techniques has introduced new variables that may alter the metastatic geography encountered on positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT). Purpose This structured narrative review examines how modern cancer therapies, prolonged survival, and procedure-related factors have reshaped recognizable metastatic patterns and created new interpretive challenges for [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT readers. Methods A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2020 to March 2026), supplemented by landmark earlier publications. The Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) guided the review. Evidence was synthesized narratively across four domains: therapy-driven clonal evolution and organotropism, emerging atypical metastatic sites, iatrogenic dissemination, and immunotherapy-era mimics and pitfalls. Results Treatment-induced clonal selection, tracked through circulating tumor DNA, is increasingly reported as a driver of metastatic evolution toward non-classical organ sites. Atypical metastatic locations, including skeletal muscle, thyroid, and cardiac deposits, are increasingly recognized. Iatrogenic dissemination through port-site implantation (incidence 0.16-2.3%) and needle tract seeding represents a distinct, procedure-related pathway of tumor spread. Immunotherapy-related phenomena, including sarcoid-like granulomatous reactions and pseudoprogression, can mimic or obscure metastatic disease on [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT. Fibroblast activation protein inhibitor-based tracers show promise for peritoneal disease detection, where [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT underperforms. Conclusions The metastatic landscape on contemporary PET/CT is shaped by treatment pressure, survival prolongation, and procedural factors. Nuclear medicine physicians should calibrate their interpretive frameworks to these evolving realities, integrating clinical context, treatment history, and awareness of emerging metastatic patterns into routine reporting practice. Prospective validation through multi-institutional registries is warranted.

title: Molecular PET imaging of cellular senescence: from current tracers to emerging biomarker-driven strategies.
abstract: Cellular senescence is a dynamic and multifaceted biological process that contributes to aging and a wide spectrum of age-related diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders. Despite increasing recognition of its pathological significance, the ability to quantify senescence noninvasively in vivo remains a major limitation, particularly for longitudinal studies and therapeutic evaluation. Positron emission tomography (PET) offers a powerful platform to address this gap by enabling quantitative imaging of molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances have led to the development of PET radiotracers targeting senescence-associated features, including lysosomal β-galactosidase activity, cell-surface markers (uPAR), and intracellular accumulation products (lipofuscin). These first-generation approaches have established proof-of-concept for imaging senescence biology; however, they primarily reflect downstream hallmarks and have been largely evaluated in non-central nervous system (CNS) models, while their ability to quantify senescent-cell burden in naturally aged tissues and the CNS remains insufficiently established. Emerging evidence motivates the study of biomarker-driven and pathway-oriented imaging strategies that may provide complementary information about senescence-associated molecular mechanisms without necessarily offering greater biological specificity. Advances in senescence biology, including curated gene sets and insights from senotherapeutic interventions, provide a framework for identifying imaging targets based on mechanistic relevance, disease association, and ligandability. Target classes spanning nuclear architecture, epigenetic regulation, metabolic reprogramming, and DNA damage signaling represent promising avenues for next-generation tracer development. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current PET tracers for cellular senescence, discusses challenges associated with CNS translation, and proposes a biomarker-driven framework for next-generation tracer development. We further introduce a comparative target-assessment framework and a stepwise validation roadmap addressing biological specificity, quantitative clinical qualification, and multimodal biomarker integration. Together, these considerations establish a framework for developing and interpreting PET biomarkers for mechanistic studies and evaluation of senescence-targeted interventions.

title: UTR-Track: unscented trajectory reconstruction with re-identification for robust lesion tracking in endoscopy videos.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is an important imaging modality for the screening and diagnosis of diseases in the GI tract. A lesion tracking technique helps maintain the identity and location of an abnormal region over time, enabling consistent monitoring rather than independent frame-by-frame detection. However, the complex endoscopic environment as non-linear camera displacement, soft tissue deformation, and occlusions are challenges for existing Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) methods. To address these issues, we propose UTR-Track, a robust tracking framework that integrates deep state estimation with adaptive feature learning. The method introduces OSNet-DCN, which embeds Deformable Convolutions into an Omni-Scale Network to extract deformation-robust features, coupled with a dual-tracker architecture, named VTA-TL-UKF. This VTA-TL-UKF utilizes an Unscented Kalman Filter with transfer-learning-based covariance stabilization and a Virtual Trajectory Augmentation module to recover fragmented tracks. Extensive experiments on self-collected clinical sequences and a public Hyper-Kvasir dataset with five types of the lesions such as gastric cancer (GC), esophageal cancer (EC), duodenal bulb ulcer (DBU), reflux esophagitis (RE), and gastritis, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On the 18 annotated IGH evaluation sequence, using the primary configuration, pairing the tracker with the hybrid-trained appearance model OSNet-DCN[Formula: see text], UTR-Track reaches a Multi-Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) of 45.4% and an IDF1 score of 74.2%. The proposed tracker eliminates identity switches IDs = 0 while improving recall (60.6%) and precision (79.9%), significantly enhancing track continuity for longitudinal lesion monitoring. These results suggest that UTR-Track effectively bridges the gap between static detection and temporally consistent tracking, supporting more reliable computer-aided diagnosis in endoscopy. Code and results are available at: https://github.com/shredder0812/UTR-Track .

title: Mask-aware knowledge distillation for low-latency pneumothorax classification in chest radiographs.
abstract: Accurate pneumothorax classification requires strong discrimination with low deployment cost. We developed a mask-aware knowledge distillation framework in which a mask-guided ResNet-50 teacher transferred dynamically annealed logits and lesion-weighted multilevel attention to a MobileNetV3-Small student, while masks and teacher-side components were removed at inference. A fixed stratified 20% SIIM-ACR hold-out set was reserved for testing; the remainder underwent five-fold cross-validation, with PTX-498 positives used only for training augmentation. The Mask-aware KD student achieved a mean validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of [Formula: see text], and the five-model student ensemble achieved a fixed-test AUC of 0.946 (95% confidence interval, 0.935-0.956) versus 0.950 for the teacher ensemble. Validation-selected 90% and 95% sensitivity targets yielded test sensitivities of 0.929 and 0.973. Uniform-attention KD achieved a lower AUC of 0.936. The student ensemble required 5.00 million parameters, 1.49 billion multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), and 51.00-ms single-threaded CPU latency at [Formula: see text]. Training-time lesion guidance enabled numerically similar discrimination with substantially lower inference cost. No independent external validation was performed, and generalizability across institutions, acquisition protocols, portable radiography settings, and patient populations remains uncertain; verified patient-level evaluation remains necessary before clinical translation.

title: Free-breathing cardiac T1 mapping registration with PCA low-rank and physics-informed constraints.
abstract: Cardiac T1 mapping is an important quantitative MRI technique for evaluating myocardial tissue properties, with significant clinical value in the early diagnosis of cardiovascular diseases. Motion correction of free-breathing T1 mapping sequences via image registration enables high-quality quantitative T1 imaging without breath-holding. However, the large non-rigid deformations caused by cardiac and respiratory motion, combined with substantial signal intensity variations across different inversion times, make it challenging for both traditional methods and existing deep learning registration models to accurately capture inter-frame structural correspondences.Therefore, we propose an unsupervised deep learning cardiac image registration method combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based low-rank constraints with physical priors. The method employs a PCA implicit global constraint to project the registered sequence onto a low-dimensional subspace for global sequence alignment, while a physical prior derived from the T1 relaxation equation synthesizes images conforming to the expected signal decay pattern to enforce consistency between registration results and the physical model. Experiments were conducted on a public STONE dataset comprising 210 patients. The proposed method achieved an average Dice coefficient of 0.843, demonstrating its accuracy and robustness under motion and contrast variations.

title: Decoding tumor heterogeneity using MRI for predicting response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in hepatocellular carcinoma: a multicenter study.
abstract: Purpose Tumor heterogeneity hinders accurate prediction of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We developed a habitat model using routine in-phase (IP) and opposed-phase (OP) MRI sequences, which provide complementary structure- and lipid-related information, to predict response to ICI therapy in HCC. Methods This study included 883 HCC patients from six institutions and public databases. We developed habitat, radiomics, peritumoral, clinical, and combined models to predict partial response (PR) in five institutions. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to evaluate survival differences based on prediction scores. Habitat model interpretability was assessed using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) along with multi-omics and pathological analyses in the public databases and one external institution. Results The habitat model showed numerically higher AUCs among the independent models, with AUCs of 0.923, 0.918, and 0.897 in the training set and two external validation sets, respectively. The combined model also showed favorable performance with AUCs of 0.959, 0.965, and 0.955, respectively. Calibration curves showed generally close agreement, while decision curve analyses suggested potential clinical net benefit of the habitat and combined models. Patients with higher habitat scores had significantly longer progression‑free and overall survival (all P < 0.05). Exploratory biological analyses showed that the higher habitat score group was associated with enhanced immune activity, downregulated fatty acid-related pathways, and shorter tumor-inflammatory spatial distances. Conclusion The IP and OP MRI-based habitat model showed potential for treatment-response prediction and prognostic stratification in patients with HCC receiving ICI therapy.

title: CT attenuation changes across freeze-thaw preservation states in donated bodies: a preliminary multi-organ anatomical analysis.
abstract: Purpose To establish the thermal preservation state as a critical pre-analytical variable in quantitative post-mortem CT of donated bodies, with the aim of enabling reliable multi-donor comparisons, improving the performance of automated segmentation tools, and providing a translational experimental model applicable to CT-guided thermal interventions. Material and methods Eight body donors underwent whole-body CT in up to three preservation states: fresh, frozen (- 20 °C), and thawed. CT datasets were automatically segmented using TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer. Mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values were extracted for major organs and tissue groups. The primary analysis was within-donor: Friedman tests with Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons in donors with complete data (n = 7), complemented by linear mixed-effects models using all available scans. Results Freezing produced a consistent reduction in CT attenuation across all soft tissues and muscle, with near-complete recovery after thawing. In the primary repeated-measures analysis, preservation state had a significant effect after FDR correction in six of the nine tissue groups (liver, spleen, brain, aorta, pancreas and muscle; q = 0.023-0.042), but not in kidney, heart or bone. Brain and pancreas showed the strongest effects (Kendall's W = 0.80 and 0.76). In the liver, the median within-donor change was - 59.7 HU at freezing and + 60.3 HU at thawing. Mixed-effects models confirmed a significant reduction at freezing in liver, spleen, brain, kidney, pancreas and muscle (β = -35.1 to -52.7 HU) and no residual difference after thawing in any tissue group. Bone attenuation remained stable across all preservation states. Conclusion Freeze-thaw preservation systematically alters CT attenuation in soft tissues while minimally affecting bone. Preservation state should therefore be considered a critical pre-analytical variable in quantitative post-mortem CT, particularly for studies relying on automated segmentation, radiomics, and translational applications involving thermal tissue imaging.

title: Enhancing brain metastasis detection on contrast-enhanced CT: the impact of maximum intensity projection (MIP) among radiologists with different levels of expertise.
abstract: Purpose Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults, pivotal for staging/treatment. Although MRI is the gold standard, contrast-enhanced brain CT is frequently used during oncologic follow-up, often interpreted by general radiologists. Maximum intensity projection (MIP) is a CT post-processing technique widely used in thoracic and vascular imaging but underexplored in neuro-oncology. We evaluated whether CT-MIP improves lesion detection according to reader expertise, metastatic burden, and lesion size. Materials and methods Retrospective single-center study of 98 patients who underwent brain MRI within 30 days of contrast-enhanced whole-body CT. Four readers (two general radiologists, two neuroradiologists) reviewed CT examinations using conventional images and CT-MIP (7-mm slabs). Primary endpoint was lesion count. Subgroup analyses were performed according to metastatic burden (oligometastatic disease) and lesion size ( < 5 mm). Secondary endpoints included interpretation time and lesion size assessment. Results Overall, MRI yielded higher lesion counts than conventional CT and CT-MIP (both p < 0.001). CT-MIP significantly increased lesion counts compared with CT for all readers (p < 0.05). In oligometastatic patients, CT-MIP showed a smaller discrepancy from MRI for general radiologists than in higher-burden cases (p < 0.001), yielding results comparable to neuroradiologists using conventional CT. CT-MIP significantly improved detection in patients with at least one metastasis < 5 mm, regardless of expertise, and reduced interpretation time. Conclusion CT-MIP improves CT-based detection of brain metastases, particularly among less-experienced readers, reducing the performance gap with neuroradiologists and providing lesion counts closer to MRI in oligometastatic disease and small metastases. While MRI remains the reference standard, CT-MIP is a simple, cost-free adjunct when MRI is unavailable or delayed.

title: MRI-guided in-bore prostate biopsy: an eight-year single-operator longitudinal experience with progressive protocol simplification and pathological validation in 1016 patients.
abstract: Objectives To describe the eight-year longitudinal performance of MRI-guided in-bore prostate biopsy performed by a single operator who began the study with limited dedicated in-bore experience; to evaluate the diagnostic equivalence of a simplified two-core sampling strategy compared with prior multi-core strategies after adjustment for temporal effects; and to provide pathological validation in a propensity-matched radical prostatectomy cohort. Materials and methods This single-centre retrospective cohort study included 1016 consecutive men with PI-RADS 3-5 lesions who underwent MRI-guided in-bore biopsy (targeted cores only, without concurrent systematic sampling) between November 2017 and November 2025. By design, all procedures were performed by one interventional radiologist on the same 1.5-T scanner (one major software upgrade in 2021), with three sequential sampling protocols (four-core, n = 185; three-core, n = 549; two-core, n = 282). Performance was assessed across five chronological quintiles. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for chronological quintile and clinical/imaging covariates. A propensity-matched radical prostatectomy cohort (n = 180) provided pathological reference. Results Overall cancer detection was 76.9% (781/1016). Across chronological quintiles, cancer detection increased from 72.9% to 78.9% (P = .04), targeting accuracy from 87.2 to 96.1% (P < .001), and procedure time decreased from 52.4 ± 9.1 to 29.7 ± 5.8 min (P < .001). After multivariable adjustment, the two-core strategy was not independently superior to multi-core strategies for clinically significant cancer detection (adjusted detection difference 4.8%, 95% CI: - 1.9% to 11.5%, P = .16), a result compatible with non-inferiority (margin 5 percentage points) rather than with superiority. In the propensity-matched surgical cohort, Gleason concordance (73-78%) and missed-cancer rates (3-5%) did not differ across strategies. Among 220 cancer-positive two-core cases, intra-biopsy Gleason concordance between central and peripheral cores was 70.0%. Conclusion In this single-operator longitudinal experience, MRI-guided in-bore biopsy performance improved substantially over time. Apparent advantages of the simplified two-core strategy largely reflected accumulating operator experience rather than intrinsic sampling strategy superiority; preserved pathological accuracy supports its non-inferiority and efficiency once proficiency is achieved. Clinical relevance statement Sequential implementation of MRI-targeted biopsy protocols can be substantially confounded by accumulating operator experience; in expert single-operator settings, a simplified two-core central-peripheral sampling strategy can match the diagnostic accuracy of multi-core approaches while reducing procedure time.

title: From detection to clinical comprehension: a cognitive hierarchy for the epistemic and ethical limits of artificial intelligence in radiology.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) detects findings in medical images at a level that, for specific tasks, matches or exceeds that of an expert radiologist. Detecting a finding, however, is not the same as understanding a disease. AI radiology literature rarely distinguishes between these two processes. This article proposes a four-level cognitive hierarchy, inspired by Ackoff's [1] model of data, information, knowledge, and wisdom, to analyze at which level current AI operates and its epistemic and ethical consequences. The four levels, detection, classification, diagnosis, and clinical comprehension, form a gradient of increasing cognitive demand. The last of these corresponds to the tacit knowledge described by Polanyi [2] and is consistent with classic studies of radiological perception. Recent literature on epistemic authority in medicine suggests that the gap between this level and AI reflects, at least in part, a difference in the type of justification underpinning clinical judgment. AI reliably automates the first two levels, makes partial progress on the third when structured clinical data are available, and currently lacks an operational counterpart for the fourth. This distinction has implications for the training of specialists and for clinical responsibility, which remains with the radiologist in AI-assisted diagnosis.

title: RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models.
abstract: Purpose Variability in chest X-ray (CXR) reporting hinders training and evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology report generation. Our previous study showed that Structured Radiology Report Generation (SRRG)-style supervision improves VLM-based CXR reporting over free-text supervision. Here, we examine this finding in a larger multi-institutional setting and address a key preprocessing challenge: reliable free-text-to-structured-report conversion using open-source small language models (SLMs). Methods We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-3B using free-text and SRRG-style structured supervision across 10 institutions covering 97K samples. We then propose RadStructAgent, an agentic framework that converts free-text CXR reports into structured reports using SLMs, combining LLM-based orchestration, judge feedback, and feedback-guided revision. RadStructAgent is evaluated on 1,000 free-text CXR reports using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. Results For the report generation task, structured supervision improves Qwen2.5-VL-3B over free-text supervision, increasing GREEN from 0.494 to 0.539, with similar gains across other clinical metrics. For the structuring task, RadStructAgent improves both clinical quality (GREEN) and anatomy-level assignment (RadFAA): for Qwen3-4B, from 0.844 to 0.867 and 0.883 to 0.891; for Qwen3-8B, from 0.863 to 0.881 and 0.889 to 0.902. Conclusion Structured supervision remains effective for VLM-based CXR report generation when evaluated in a larger multi-institutional setting. RadStructAgent shows that open-source SLMs can be strengthened through agentic verification and refinement, providing a resource-efficient approach for offline and privacy-preserving structured report preparation. Our code, prompt templates, and configuration files are publicly available at: https://github.com/badhon1512/RadStructAgent .

title: Integration of weight-bearing computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for advanced musculoskeletal statistical shape modeling of the foot and ankle.
abstract: Purpose Statistical shape models (SSMs) from three-dimensional (3D) medical imaging describe morphology variation in normal and pathologic anatomy. Within the foot and ankle, weight-bearing computed tomography (WBCT) is used to characterize skeletal deformity but poorly visualizes soft tissue. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides improved evaluation of soft tissue structures but less accurate bone visualization. This methodologic analysis describes and tests reliability of a novel process to generate SSMs from coregistered MRI and WBCT structures. This method is illustrated via two example models: a combined musculoskeletal model and a distal tibia growth plate model. Methods Bilateral WBCTs and T1-weighted DIXON MRIs of the lower legs were collected from 14 individuals aged 8 to 18 with no prior lower limb surgery in a control group and hereditary neuropathy group. Bones were segmented from WBCT and manually aligned in MRI space. Alignment reliability was evaluated with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Six muscles were segmented semi-automatically and the distal tibia growth plate was manually segmented from MRI. Following cropping, size normalization, and alignment multi-domain SSMs were generated. SSMs were evaluated qualitatively through comparison with expected anatomy and quantitively by calculation of compactness, generalization, and specificity. Results The alignment method demonstrated excellent reliability with an intrarater ICC of 1 and interrater ICC of 0.999. The musculoskeletal model demonstrated expected atrophy in neuromuscular disease and the preliminary growth plate model showed variation in metaphyseal thickness. Both models demonstrated compactness, specificity, and generalization comparable to published SSMs, requiring 11 and 12 modes to account for 95% of population variance. Conclusion This method allows for application of shape modeling to novel questions in musculoskeletal morphology through simultaneous modeling of bone and soft tissue anatomy. Limitations include manual registration and MRI resolution. This analysis presented examples of muscle and growth plate models, but has broader applications in musculoskeletal analysis.

title: Projection restoration with dual-domain Swin refinement for sparse-view CT reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose We investigated whether projection restoration before reconstruction, followed by image-domain refinement, improves sparse-view computed tomography (CT) quality under aggressive undersampling. Methods A compact dual-domain Swin framework restores sparse sinograms before geometry-aware differentiable filtered back projection (FBP) and refines the resulting images. The projection branch uses gated Swin processing and angular upsampling with a bicubic bypass. Abdominal AAPM sinograms contained 2304 full views, retaining 576, 288, and 144 views at 4x, 8x, and 16x. Comparators were FBP, bilinear and bicubic interpolation, ProCT, and geometry-adapted DuDoTrans; ablations used ten epochs. Results DuDoSwin achieved PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS of 45.64 dB/0.981/0.011 at 4x, 44.11 dB/0.975/0.020 at 8x, and 42.02 dB/0.963/0.035 at 16x. Mean PSNR and SSIM exceeded ProCT and DuDoTrans; DuDoTrans had lower LPIPS at 4x and 8x. DuDoSwin used 1.36-1.80 million parameters but was slower than both learned comparators. Comparisons against interpolation and DuDoTrans were significant in Holm-corrected paired tests. Bypass removal improved ablation PSNR by 0.35 dB at 8x. Evaluation included the validation patient; exclusion changed mean PSNR by at most 0.1 dB and altered no ranking. Slice-wise tests ignore within-patient dependence. Conclusion Explicit projection restoration followed by image-domain refinement yielded favorable PSNR and SSIM, with perceptual metric and computational trade-offs. Neither residual shortcut improved the 8x ablation results. Independent patient evaluation remains necessary.
