Models included changes in NITs (dichotomized by Youden index) chosen by the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator with 3-fold cross-validation.

Results

Participants who received survodutide had improvements in all assessed NITs vs placebo. Changes in MRI-PDFF (relative importance to the prediction: 100%), ELF™ (61.9%), and FAST score (50.4%) were predictive of resolution of MASH with no worsening of fibrosis (full dataset: AUC 0.85, 95% CI, 0.78-0.93, P<.0001; AUC based on cross-validation: 0.84). Changes in ELF™ (100%), ALT (87.2%), PRO-C3 (76.3%), MRI-PDFF (75.6%), FAST score (72.3%), Agile 3+ (50.5%), and CAP™ (13.6%) were predictive of improvement of fibrosis with no worsening of MASH (full dataset: AUC 0.81, 95% CI, 0.73-0.90, P<.0001; AUC based on cross-validation: 0.76).

Conclusion

Changes in MRI-PDFF, ELF™ score, and FAST score were identified as the most important for prediction of the 2 biopsy outcomes. Larger datasets are needed to enhance model accuracy and refinement.

title: Pulmonary Function Estimation from Opportunistic Chest CT Using a Hybrid Image-plus-Quantitative-Feature Deep Learning Model.
abstract: Background Spirometry is underused and most airflow obstruction remains undiagnosed. Chest CT acquired for lung cancer screening contains anatomical and densitometric information that may proxy lung function. Research question Can a deep learning model combining volumetric CT with CT-derived quantitative features estimate spirometric parameters and detect abnormal spirometry in independent external cohorts without retraining? Study design and methods A three-dimensional convolutional neural network trained on 10,371 low-dose CT reconstructions from 5,975 National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) participants was fused with 20 lung densitometry and tracheal geometry features to predict FEV 1 , FVC and FEV 1 /FVC. The frozen model was applied to an External Lung Cancer Screening Cohort (ELCSC, n = 268) and COPDGene (n = 10,302 scans). Ablation, two spirometric-pattern subgroups and prevalence-conditional predictive values were also evaluated. Reference spirometry was pre-bronchodilator in NLST and post-bronchodilator in COPDGene. Abnormal spirometry (FEV 1 /FVC < 0.70, FEV 1 < 80% or FVC < 80% predicted) was assessed with sensitivity, specificity and AUROC, and agreement with the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). Results The model detected abnormal spirometry with AUROC 0.898 (sensitivity 89.9%, specificity 66.1%) in the ELCSC and AUROC 0.913 (sensitivity 66.9%, specificity 96.3%) in COPDGene, with CCCs of 0.80-0.88 for FEV 1 , FVC and FEV 1 /FVC. In held-out development data, CCCs were 0.86/0.85/0.71 (full model) versus 0.83/0.82/0.50 image-only and 0.55/0.65/0.35 feature-only. Agreement was lower, with systematic overestimation, in a COPD subgroup (FEV 1 /FVC < 0.70; CCC 0.62) and in a low-FVC, preserved-ratio pattern (CCC 0.70-0.78). Interpretation The model estimates spirometric parameters and detects abnormal spirometry across independent cohorts without retraining, with different sensitivity-specificity profiles at the same decision rule. It shows promise for opportunistic assessment of existing CT scans, but referral performance varies by population and prospective utility is unproven. Clinical trial registration COPDGene, ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT00608764.

title: Effect of soft contact lens correction on quantitative OCT and OCT angiography measurements in high myopia: A prospective paired study.
abstract: Purpose To determine whether soft contact lens correction alters quantitative optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), macular optical coherence tomography (OCT), and optic nerve head measurements in highly myopic eyes. Methods Twenty patients with cycloplegic spherical refraction of -6.00 D or more myopic underwent swept-source OCT/OCTA with the DRI OCT Triton 3D Plus. Macular 6 × 6-mm and optic disc scans were acquired first without a contact lens using internal refractive compensation and then repeated through an ACUVUE OASYS spherical soft contact lens. SCP and DCP vessel density, image quality, macular structural variables, optic disc morphometry, and sectoral RNFL thickness were compared using participant-level paired change scores. False discovery rate (FDR) was controlled with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Results Thirty-eight eyes of 20 patients were analyzed (mean age 26.95 ± 6.32 years; mean spherical refraction -7.49 ± 1.48 D). Contact lens correction reduced OCTA quality and SCP vessel density in the central, superior, temporal, and nasal regions (all FDR-adjusted q < 0.05). Central DCP vessel density decreased, whereas inferior DCP vessel density increased. Retinal thickness decreased modestly, inferior RNFL thickness increased, and optic disc quality decreased; most global structural parameters remained stable. Conclusions Soft contact lens correction systematically influenced selected quantitative OCT/OCTA measurements in high myopia. The concurrent reduction in scan quality and several vessel-density measurements suggests an important optical or acquisition-related component. Longitudinal OCT/OCTA examinations should therefore use a consistent refractive correction condition.

title: Postoperative midline shift and functional outcome after surgery for chronic subdural hematoma.
abstract: Background Chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) lacks well-established postoperative radiological markers associated with long-term functional outcome. We evaluated the association between postoperative midline shift (MLS) and 6-month functional outcome using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) after CSDH surgery. Methods We retrospectively analyzed prospectively collected data from 172 surgical CSDH patients. The primary prognostic analysis was restricted to unilateral CSDH (n=122) because opposing mass effects alter MLS interpretation in bilateral hematomas. The primary outcome was unfavorable 6-month functional status (mRS 3-6). A parsimonious Firth penalized logistic regression model adjusting for age, admission Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), and postoperative MLS (modeled continuously first, and as ≥5 vs. <5 mm secondarily) was fitted. Results Among 122 unilateral CSDH patients, 22 (18.0%) had an unfavorable 6-month outcome. Across 106 re-evaluated postoperative CT scans, intraobserver and interobserver reliability was excellent for continuous MLS (ICC: 0.982 and 0.985) and high for the ≥5-mm threshold (κ: 0.902 and 0.862). In the primary Firth model, continuous postoperative MLS showed a positive but imprecisely estimated association with unfavorable outcome (OR 1.16 per 1-mm increase, 95% CI 0.983-1.36; p=0.079), with an apparent c-statistic of 0.704 (95% CI 0.564-0.844) and bootstrap optimism-corrected c-statistic of 0.674. In the secondary model, postoperative MLS ≥5 mm was associated with higher odds of unfavorable outcome (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.003-7.45; p=0.049). Conclusions Higher postoperative MLS showed a consistent direction of association with unfavorable 6-month outcome in unilateral CSDH, although the continuous estimate was imprecise. These findings support postoperative MLS as a potential prognostic marker rather than a therapeutic target, though its incremental prognostic value beyond pre-morbid functional status and preoperative radiological severity remains unknown. The 5-mm threshold does not justify imaging-driven reintervention.

title: Volumetric modeling of residual meningioma growth.
abstract: Purpose Meningioma resection remains incomplete in roughly 25% of cases; improved characterization of remnant growth could help clinicians optimize postoperative management. This study aims to characterize the volumetric growth of residual meningiomas and to identify factors associated with rapid growth. Methods A retrospective cohort design was applied to adult patients with residual WHO grade 1 intracranial meningioma. Tumor volume was measured at every postoperative MRI. Tumor growth rates (TGR) were derived and clustered. Factors associated with rapid growth were explored. Fit was compared across linear, exponential, Gompertzian and power models. Model performance on untrained datapoints was assessed. Results Sixty-one (61) remnants were followed for an average of 71.1 months (SD = 41.3) postoperatively. Mean TGR was 1.79 %/month (SD = 3.51) preoperatively and 1.68 %/month (SD = 4.36) postoperatively. The fast growth cluster represented 32% of the cohort with a mean TGR of 2.71 %/month (SD = 0.93) while the slow growth cluster represented 68% of the cohort with a mean TGR of 0.20 %/month (SD = 0.70) (p < 0.001). A positive correlation was found between preoperative and postoperative TGRs (ρ= 0.713, p < 0.001). Linear and exponential models best described growth. Prediction error on untrained datapoints grew over time. Conclusion Most meningioma remnants showed slow volumetric progression, whereas approximately one-third demonstrated rapid growth. Interestingly, postoperative growth rate may be linked to preoperative growth rate. Different growth models seem to offer comparable explanatory performance, with the accuracy of predictive models remaining limited.

title: Emphysematous osteomyelitis of the lower extremity: Prevalence, imaging features, interobserver agreement and clinical outcomes in a 16-hospital cohort.
abstract: Purpose To estimate emphysematous osteomyelitis (EO) observed prevalence, compare 3-month major adverse events (death or major amputation) between EO and nonemphysematous osteomyelitis (NEO), and assess interobserver agreement for key imaging features. Methods In this retrospective 16-hospital study, radiology-report text screening followed by manual report review identified CT and MRI examinations demonstrating lower-extremity osteomyelitis. EO was defined as intraosseous gas without direct bone-to-air communication. Forty-five EO cases met criteria, and 180 NEO cases were randomly sampled in a 4:1 ratio for prognostic comparison. Associations with 3-month major adverse events were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Three radiologists independently reviewed 90 cases (45 EO, 45 NEO) to assess interobserver agreement. Results Of the 1417 imaging examinations that identified lower-extremity osteomyelitis, 45 (3.2%) met the study's EO inclusion criteria. Major adverse events occurred within 3 months in 33.3% (15/45) of EO cases and 12.8% (23/180) of nonemphysematous osteomyelitis cases. EO (adjusted OR, 3.22; 95% CI, 1.46-7.12; p = .004) and peripheral artery disease (adjusted OR, 3.11; 95% CI, 1.38-7.03; p = .006) were independently associated with higher odds of death or major amputation within 3 months. Agreement for intraosseous gas was substantial on CT (κ = 0.71) and almost perfect on MRI (κ = 0.81). Conclusion EO is uncommon but associated with worse 3-month outcomes. Our findings support consideration of EO as a potential imaging marker of short-term adverse outcomes in patients with lower-extremity osteomyelitis.

title: Toward a unified computational representation of lung cancer: from radiomics and pathomics to multimodal AI.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how lung cancer is characterized by enabling quantitative analysis of both radiologic and pathologic images. Radiomics extracts high-dimensional features from radiologic images, whereas pathomics applies analogous approaches to digitized histopathology, providing complementary representations of tumor biology across different spatial scales. Recent advances in foundation models and multimodal AI have accelerated the convergence of these disciplines, creating opportunities to integrate imaging, pathology, and molecular information within unified frameworks. In this review, we summarize the principles of radiomics and pathomics, discuss recent developments in foundation models for thoracic imaging and computational pathology, and examine emerging strategies for multimodal integration in lung cancer. Available evidence, although largely retrospective, suggests that integrated radio-pathomic models can outperform single-modality approaches for clinically complex tasks, including recurrence prediction, molecular characterization, and treatment response assessment. We also discuss the major barriers limiting clinical translation, including reproducibility, external validation, interoperability, interpretability, and regulatory implementation. Rather than replacing radiology or pathology, multimodal AI is progressively connecting both disciplines through shared computational representations of disease, supporting more comprehensive and biologically informed approaches to precision oncology.

title: Characterizing the heterogeneity of Alzheimer's disease through EEG normative modeling.
abstract: Objective To integrate normative modeling with non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) to characterize individualized brain functional abnormalities across Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), thereby elucidating disease heterogeneity and enabling biologically informed stratification. Methods We constructed sex-specific normative age models for the small-world (SW) architecture of hemispheric EEG networks and quantified individual SW deviations in 160 AD, 161 MCI, and 769 healthy controls (HCs) across multiple datasets. Individual deviation profiles were used to delineate sex-dependent topological alterations across the cognitive spectrum. We further performed unsupervised clustering to identify subtypes for both AD and MCI, and characterized their inter-subtype similarities and differences. The identified subtypes were rigorously validated for internal/external consistency and specificity. Results EEG normative models (NMs) captured frequency-specific aging trajectories of SW organization and revealed progressive sex-related divergence in SW deviation with cognitive decline. Both MCI and AD cohorts were consistently classified into two EEG-defined subtypes with distinct intrinsic dysconnectivity patterns and cognitive profiles, despite no differences in canonical multimodal MRI measures. Subtype-1 exhibited relatively preserved network organization and distinctive neurocognitive recovery patterns, whereas subtype-2 showed widespread network disruption and poorer clinical outcomes. Cross-stage analyses demonstrated shared EEG signatures between corresponding MCI and AD subtype pairs, supporting their biological continuity. Multidimensional validation confirmed the robustness and generalizability of our subtyping framework. Conclusions NM-guided EEG profiling reveals clinically meaningful neurobiological heterogeneity cross the AD spectrum and identifies a high-risk MCI subtype before detectable cerebral atrophy. Significance This framework provides an individualized, non-invasive strategy for early AD subtyping and prognostic stratification.

title: Low cross-sectional area of the geniohyoid muscle is associated with non-home discharge in older patients admitted to the emergency department.
abstract: Background and aims Functional decline and non-home discharge are common among older patients hospitalized in acute care settings and are associated with poor prognosis. Swallowing dysfunction is a key factor affecting functional recovery; however, the association between swallowing-related muscle mass and discharge outcomes remains unclear. This study investigated the association between the cross-sectional area (CSA) of the geniohyoid muscle (GH) at admission and discharge destination in older patients admitted to an acute care hospital. Methods This single-center prospective observational study included patients aged ≥65 years who were admitted from home to the emergency department, hospitalized for ≥5 days, and received rehabilitation. GH-CSA was measured within 5 days of admission using ultrasonography. Participants were classified into low and high GH-CSA groups using sex-specific cutoff values (≤194.7 mm 2 for men and ≤172.5 mm 2 for women). The primary outcome was discharge destination (home vs non-home). Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to examine the independent association between low GH-CSA and non-home discharge, adjusting for clinically relevant covariates. Model A was adjusted for age, sex, MUST score ≥2, CCI, circulatory disorders, pre-admission FOIS, pre-admission BI, and living alone, whereas Model B excluded MUST score ≥2. Results A total of 242 patients were included in the analysis. Patients with low GH-CSA had a significantly higher proportion of non-home discharge compared with those with high GH-CSA (53.9% vs 30.7%, p < 0.001). GH-CSA was significantly lower in patients discharged to non-home destinations than in those discharged home (median, 152.2 vs. 177.1 mm 2 ; p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression analyses, low GH-CSA was independently associated with non-home discharge in both Model A (odds ratio [OR] 2.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15-4.24; p = 0.017) and Model B (OR 2.63, 95% CI 1.40-4.95; p = 0.003). Conclusions Low GH-CSA at admission was independently associated with non-home discharge among older patients hospitalized in an acute care setting. Ultrasound assessment of GH-CSA may serve as a simple and objective marker for early identification of patients at high risk of adverse discharge outcomes.

title: Application of the quantum reconstruction method to the geometry of a commercial CT scanner.
abstract: Background and objective This paper introduces a novel quantum-based approach to image reconstruction in practical computed tomography, particularly for spiral scanners equipped with the Flying Focal Spot technique. The main objective of this study is to demonstrate the feasibility of applying an abstract quantum reconstruction method to the real geometric configuration of clinical scanners. The complex geometry of projection rays in such systems substantially limits the applicability of conventional reconstruction techniques, as well as statistical methods based on discrete-to-discrete data models. Methods The experimental evaluation was conducted using physical projection data acquired from a commercial scanner. A comparative analysis was performed between the proposed method and a conventional filtered reconstruction algorithm, employing objective image quality metrics. Results The experimental results indicate that the proposed approach overcomes several limitations of traditional reconstruction methods in terms of implementation possibilities and obtained image quality. Moreover, it demonstrates potential for reducing the X-ray dose required for computed tomography examinations. Conclusion The proposed method directly utilizes measurements obtained from the CT scanner without the need for any interpolation. The reconstruction framework incorporates a statistical iterative reconstruction strategy, classifying the method within the Model-Based Iterative Reconstruction family. The reconstruction algorithm is highly efficient, completing all computations in approximately 7-12 s on a mid-range processors. This performance is largely attributable to the use of fast Fourier transform algorithms for the most computationally intensive operations, particularly the convolution steps within the iterative process. Such efficiency is especially advantageous for ambulatory diagnostic applications.

title: LD<sup>2</sup>AL: A deep active learning framework with learnable diffusion representations for medical hyperspectral image segmentation.
abstract: Background and objective Medical hyperspectral imaging (MHSI) provides rich spectral-spatial information for precise lesion delineation. However, its high dimensionality and the substantial cost of pixel-wise annotation significantly limit the development of effective segmentation models under constrained labeling budgets. This study aims to improve annotation efficiency while maintaining high segmentation accuracy in MHSI. Methods We present LD 2 AL, a diffusion-based deep active learning framework for MHSI segmentation. The framework first learns a unified latent representation via a learnable diffusion autoencoder (LDiffAE), which jointly encodes semantic structure and imaging uncertainty in an unsupervised manner. Based on this representation, a dual-stage sample selection strategy is designed, combining angle-based outlier detection (ABOD) for representativeness pre-screening and texture complexity analysis for fine-grained ranking. Results Experiments on two gastric hyperspectral datasets (PLGC-IM and PLGC-GIN) demonstrate that LD 2 AL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art active learning methods across multiple metrics. Notably, the proposed method achieves Dice scores of 86.30% on PLGC-IM and 84.62% on PLGC-GIN with only 2500 labeled samples, while substantially reducing the annotation requirement compared with full supervision. Conclusions The proposed framework effectively reduces annotation requirements while preserving high segmentation performance. By integrating uncertainty-aware representation learning with a dual-stage selection strategy, LD 2 AL provides a practical and scalable solution for label-efficient medical hyperspectral image analysis.

title: Undersampled K-space information recovery with long-range temporal memory for multi-coil MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Background Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging through k-space undersampling introduces a challenging inverse problem: recovering the full frequency spectrum from incomplete Fourier measurements. Existing unrolled networks apply static regularization uniformly across cascades, ignoring that reconstruction challenges evolve from coarse artifact suppression to fine detail recovery. We aimed to develop a temporal memory framework that accumulates reconstruction knowledge and dynamically adapts regularization strategies. Methods Our main contribution is a cascade-wise attention-weighted memory that aggregates a buffer of recent reconstruction features through a learned, state-dependent gate, so that the regularization adapts across the unrolled cascades. We evaluated our framework on cardiac data (300 cases, 1.5T/3.0T/5.0T, nine disease categories) and knee data (197 volumes) across uniform, Gaussian, and radial undersampling at 8, 16, and 24 times acceleration. Quality was assessed using structural similarity index and peak signal-to-noise ratio. Results Our method achieved structural similarity of 0.888 and peak signal-to-noise ratio of 33.29 dB on cardiac data, outperforming PromptMR by 0.023 SSIM and 1.51 dB and also improving on HierAdaptMR, and ranking among the top teams in the CMRxRecon2025 challenge. On knee data at 24 times acceleration, improvements reached 0.094 for uniform and 0.127 for radial undersampling. Performance gains increased with reconstruction difficulty. Conclusions Long-range temporal memory enables cascade-adaptive k-space recovery, providing substantial benefits precisely when reconstruction becomes severely ill-posed, with consistent improvements across two anatomies and several undersampling patterns, using a separately trained model for each anatomy. Code available at https://github.com/Ruru-Xu/cmr-temporal-memory.

title: DMM-Net: A dual-stage multimodal modulation network for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
abstract: Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) typically progresses from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and eventually to AD. Due to the overlap of imaging manifestations and clinical indicators across different stages, accurate multi-class diagnosis remains challenging. Although structured clinical data can provide complementary information to imaging modalities, effective collaborative modeling between three-dimensional structural magnetic resonance imaging (3D sMRI) and structured clinical data remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to develop a cross-modal modulation approach for AD diagnosis. Methods In this study, a Dual-stage Multimodal Modulation Network (DMM-Net) was proposed for AD cognitive state classification by integrating 3D sMRI and structured clinical data. The proposed framework consists of a Position-aware Clinical Spatial Modulation (PCSM) module, a transfer learning-based three-dimensional imaging feature extraction network MedNet, and a Feature-Clinical Cross-modal Modulation (FCCM) module. At the shallow stage, PCSM combines an image-derived spatial response with a subject-level clinical bias to modulate early imaging features. At deeper stages, FCCM jointly uses the intermediate Layer2 imaging representation and the clinical embedding to generate stage-specific calibration parameters for Layer3 and Layer4. Results Experimental results on the ADNI dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of DMM-Net for the CN/MCI/AD three-class classification task. The combined PCSM-FCCM configuration achieved a BA of 75.1%, outperforming either module alone. Compared with the adapted HyperFusion baseline under the unified evaluation protocol, DMM-Net improved BA and precision by 9.0 and 7.7 percentage points, respectively. Post hoc Grad-CAM and SHAP analyses were used to characterize the imaging regions and structured clinical features associated with the model predictions. Conclusion The framework enhances joint modeling between 3D sMRI and structured clinical data through a coordinated dual-stage multimodal modulation mechanism, demonstrating its effectiveness for multimodal computer-aided classification of Alzheimer's disease under the evaluated setting.

title: Domain shift-aware evaluation of deep learning and radiomics-based machine learning in multi-vendor mammography.
abstract: Background and objectives Artificial intelligence models for mammography are commonly developed under relatively homogeneous data conditions but are increasingly expected to operate across heterogeneous imaging environments, where domain shifts can substantially degrade performance. The comparative domain-shift robustness of radiomics-based machine learning and CNN-based deep learning models remains insufficiently characterized. This study aims to establish a controlled baseline robustness evaluation comparing radiomics-based machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models across a progressive multivendor domain-shift hierarchy. Methods We evaluated 80 model configurations comprising ML and DL architectures under three training strategies. Stratified five-fold cross-validation was performed using mammography datasets from two vendors (GE and Hologic) for same-vendor and cross-vendor evaluation, with CBIS-DDSM used as an external technology-shift stress test. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve with 95% confidence intervals, along with error profiles including sensitivity and specificity. Performance trajectories were characterized at both the best-performing model and model-family average levels. Model interpretability was evaluated using Shapley additive explanations for ML and gradient-weighted class activation mapping for DL. Results Under same-vendor conditions, ML achieved slightly higher AUCs than DL on both datasets (GE: AUC 0.96 vs. 0.94; Hologic: AUC 0.89 vs. 0.87). Cross-vendor evaluation demonstrated direction-dependent transfer asymmetry: both paradigms achieved comparable AUCs within each transfer direction (Hologic-to-GE: AUC 0.94; GE-to-Hologic: AUC 0.83), with paradigm-specific error profiles differing within each direction. Model-family trajectory analysis showed larger average AUC declines for ML than for DL as domain distance increased (cross-vendor: 6.04% vs. 2.23%; stress test: 36.58% vs. 25.33%). Under the external technology-shift stress test, DL showed attenuated performance degradation compared with ML under combined training (AUC 0.72 vs. 0.61), whereas ML exhibited pronounced specificity collapse. Conclusions Radiomics-based ML achieved strong same-vendor performance and interpretable feature attributions, whereas CNN-based DL demonstrated relatively attenuated performance degradation under increasing domain distance, particularly in the stress-test setting and after combined multivendor training. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating AI systems not only by overall discrimination performance but also by vendor-specific error profiles and cross-vendor performance stability, to inform domain-aware validation and clinical translation in heterogeneous mammography environments.

Artificial intelligence models for mammography are commonly developed under relatively homogeneous data conditions but are increasingly expected to operate across heterogeneous imaging environments, where domain shifts can substantially degrade performance. This study aims to establish a controlled baseline robustness evaluation comparing radiomics-based machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models across a progressive multivendor domain-shift hierarchy.

Methods

We evaluated 80 model configurations comprising ML and DL architectures under three training strategies. Stratified five-fold cross-validation was performed using mammography datasets from two vendors (GE and Hologic) for same-vendor and cross-vendor evaluation, with CBIS-DDSM used as an external technology-shift stress test. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve with 95% confidence intervals, along with error profiles including sensitivity and specificity. Performance trajectories were characterized at both the best-performing model and model-family average levels. Model interpretability was evaluated using Shapley additive explanations for ML and gradient-weighted class activation mapping for DL.

Results

Under same-vendor conditions, ML achieved slightly higher AUCs than DL on both datasets (GE: AUC 0.96 vs. 0.94; Hologic: AUC 0.89 vs. 0.87). Cross-vendor evaluation demonstrated direction-dependent transfer asymmetry: both paradigms achieved comparable AUCs within each transfer direction (Hologic-to-GE: AUC 0.94; GE-to-Hologic: AUC 0.83), with paradigm-specific error profiles differing within each direction. Model-family trajectory analysis showed larger average AUC declines for ML than for DL as domain distance increased (cross-vendor: 6.04% vs. 2.23%; stress test: 36.58% vs. 25.33%). Under the external technology-shift stress test, DL showed attenuated performance degradation compared with ML under combined training (AUC 0.72 vs. 0.61), whereas ML exhibited pronounced specificity collapse.

Conclusions

Radiomics-based ML achieved strong same-vendor performance and interpretable feature attributions, whereas CNN-based DL demonstrated relatively attenuated performance degradation under increasing domain distance, particularly in the stress-test setting and after combined multivendor training. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating AI systems not only by overall discrimination performance but also by vendor-specific error profiles and cross-vendor performance stability, to inform domain-aware validation and clinical translation in heterogeneous mammography environments.

title: fastrad: Complete, IBSI-Validated GPU Acceleration of the Full PyRadiomics Feature Set.
abstract: Background and objective Radiomic feature extraction is a critical step in quantitative medical imaging pipelines. The reference implementation, PyRadiomics, runs only on the central processing unit, and existing GPU-accelerated alternatives cover at most two of the eight standardised radiomic feature classes without reported numerical validation against PyRadiomics. This work introduces fastrad, a GPU-native Python library implementing all eight PyRadiomics-compatible feature classes in PyTorch, evaluated under a dual-validation design: conformity to Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) reference values, and feature-level parity with PyRadiomics under matched extraction settings. Methods Images and masks are cropped to the region of interest (ROI) before any computation, and all feature classes run on PyTorch tensors on the CPU or a CUDA GPU. Correctness was evaluated against the IBSI Phase 1 digital phantom (107 features, seven classes) and against PyRadiomics on six clinical CT cases from the TCIA NSCLC-Radiomics collection. Single-scan extraction time was measured as one full extraction call per timing (median of 20 runs) on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 and an Intel Core i9-14900KF, against single- and 32-thread PyRadiomics. Cohort throughput was compared between PyRadiomics on 32 CPU processes and fastrad on one GPU with a VRAM-aware number of concurrent workers. Scan-rescan reproducibility was assessed on 10 RIDER Lung CT pairs with ICC(2,1). Results fastrad met the IBSI Phase 1 criterion for all 107 features (maximum relative deviation 1.46×10 -13 %) and agreed with PyRadiomics for all 107 features on all six clinical cases (largest absolute difference 3.2×10 -9 on the primary case). Exact shape agreement required computing the marching-cubes mesh in PyRadiomics' coordinate frame, because the mesh is not always closed and the volume of an open mesh depends on the origin. On the primary case (56,637 voxels) one extraction took 29.2 ms on the GPU and 0.22 s on one CPU thread, versus 2.72 s for single-thread and 1.83 s for 32-thread PyRadiomics: 62-fold faster than PyRadiomics' fastest configuration. Cohort throughput on one GPU reached 2020 scans/min with 10 concurrent workers, 4.3 times that of 32-process PyRadiomics (468 scans/min). ICC values of the two tools were identical to seven decimal places for all features. Conclusions Within the evaluated feature classes, hardware and settings, fastrad reproduces PyRadiomics feature values to floating-point precision while reducing single-scan extraction time by more than an order of magnitude on the CPU and nearly two orders of magnitude on a consumer GPU, and it exceeds a fully occupied 32-thread CPU in cohort throughput on one GPU. fastrad is openly available on PyPI and GitHub under the Apache 2.0 licence.

title: Development of mobile-deployable vision language models for layman chest radiograph summarization using parameter-efficient fine-tuning and quantization.
abstract: Background and objective Chest radiography is among the most widely performed diagnostic imaging procedures in clinical medicine, yet the technical reports generated by radiologists often remain incomprehensible to patients. Automated generation of patient-friendly layman summaries from chest X-ray images and radiology reports using vision-language models represents a clinically viable solution. However, the feasibility of deploying such models on consumer mobile devices remains undemonstrated, limiting their applicability in resource-limited settings and LMICs where cloud infrastructure cannot be assumed. This study aimed to investigate whether a compact vision-language model, fine-tuned using parameter-efficient methods, can be deployed on a smartphone while approaching the performance of substantially larger models. Methods Four vision-language models of increasing size, namely Gemma3 (4B), Qwen3-VL (8B), Llama 3.2 Vision (11B), and Pixtral-2409 (12B), were evaluated under pre-trained and fine-tuned Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) conditions on over 130,000 chest X-ray image-radiology-layman report triplets from the PadChest corpus. Evaluation spanned text relevance (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore, semantic similarity), linguistic readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Coleman-Liau Index, Dale-Chall Readability Score), and clinical fidelity (RadGraph-F1). Zero-shot generalization was assessed on an external MIMIC-CXR validation set, alongside a report-only ablation study. A clinical radiologist independently assessed outputs from the fine-tuned compact model using a five-point Likert scale across accuracy, completeness, conciseness, and safety criteria. Results Fine-tuning produced transformative gains across all models. BLEU improved by up to 12-fold, ROUGE-2 6.7-fold, and RadGraph-F1 4.8-fold. Readability shifted from a college-level baseline average of FKGL 12.72 and CLI 13.63 to consistently patient-appropriate levels averaging FKGL 7.49 and CLI 8.67 across the models. Post fine-tuning, inter-model differences remained around 0.12 on BLEU, under 0.09 on FKGL, and approximately 0.09 on RadGraph-F1. External validation preserved clinical fidelity (RadGraph-F1 0.373), and a report-only ablation confirmed the radiograph's contribution. Radiologist evaluation yielded a Likert score of 4.76/5.00, indicating promising clinical quality. The model was deployed on a consumer smartphone via GGUF quantization at a throughput of 18.26 tokens per second. Conclusion Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a compact 4-billion-parameter vision-language model yields performance approaching that of models 3 times its size for layman chest radiograph summarization. Deployment on a consumer smartphone at clinically viable inference speeds establishes on-device radiology report simplification as a practical reality.

title: A theranostic latent representation framework for multi-lesion aggregation and heterogeneity quantification: application to multicenter ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE SPECT/CT imaging.
abstract: Purpose Multicenter radiomics studies in SPECT/CT imaging are highly susceptible to variability arising from differences in acquisition protocols, reconstruction settings, and scanner characteristics, which can obscure underlying biological signals. We aimed to develop a harmonized latent representation framework to improve robustness, interpretability, and patient-level modeling in theranostic imaging. Materials and methods A retrospective multicenter dataset comprising 50 patients and 499 lesion-level records from ¹⁷⁷Lu-DOTATATE SPECT/CT imaging at three institutions was analyzed. A total of 93 lesion-level radiomic features, including first-order statistic, texture and non-uniformity descriptors reflecting intra-lesion heterogeneity, were extracted from lesion-level segmentations following IBSI guidelines. Feature-level harmonization was performed using ComBat to mitigate center-related variability. Subsequently, principal component analysis was applied to construct a low-dimensional latent space. Lesion phenotypes were identified via clustering, and patient-level latent representations were derived by aggregating lesion-level embeddings to capture intra-patient inter-lesion variability. For single-lesion patients, the latent aggregation reduces to the corresponding lesion-level embedding. A perturbation-based simulation framework was further employed to evaluate latent-space stability and dynamic behavior. Results ComBat reduced center-related variance substantially, with η² decreasing from up to 0.75 pre-harmonization to ∼0.000-0.006 post-harmonization. Latent correlations showed increased alignment with the intensity proxy (0.351 to 0.956) and decreased alignment with the texture proxy (0.967 to 0.528). Clustering revealed greater variation across phenotypes than across centers in the harmonized latent space. Patient-level heterogeneity indices varied independently of lesion count. Perturbation analysis showed low phenotype transition rates (<10%) and smooth centroid shifts, confirming both stability and sensitivity of the latent space. Conclusion The proposed framework enables robust multicenter radiomics by integrating harmonization and latent modeling. The resulting theranostic latent representation supports biologically meaningful characterization and simulation-driven exploration, advancing toward digital twin applications.

title: Eu-doped gadolinium fluoride nanoparticles as MRI active theranostic agent with pronounced radiocatalytic activity.
abstract: Radiotherapy remains one of the most widely used and effective methods for tumor treatment. Nanoparticle-based sensitizers are regarded as promising tools in radiotherapy since they can enhance therapeutic efficacy while reducing adverse side effects. Due to their large X-ray absorption cross-section and high proton beam stopping power, lanthanide fluoride nanoparticles have attracted considerable attention as potential radiosensitizers. In this study, we synthesized europium-doped (5, 10 and 20 mass %) gadolinium fluoride nanoparticles (GdEuF 3 NPs) and evaluated their radiocatalytic activity under X-ray and proton beam irradiation. Additionally, we performed comprehensive analysis of their cytotoxicity (IC50) and bioactivity using 4 different cell lines (3 cancer and 1 normal cell lines). The synthesized GdEuF 3 NPs demonstrated not only high colloidal stability, but also pronounced MRI contrast properties exceeding commercial MRI contrast agents (Gadobutrol®). The GdEuF 3 NPs exhibited pH-dependent radiocatalytic activity, which was predominantly observed under acidic conditions (pH 6.5) under proton beam irradiation, while a weaker effect was detected at neutral pH under X-ray irradiation. The GdEuF 3 NPs were highly biocompatible with the 4T1, MNNG/Hos, EMT6/P, and NCTC L929 cell lines over a wide concentration range (10-100 μg/mL) and across different europium contents, with no detectable adverse effects. Taking into account the pH-dependent radiation-induced overgeneration of ROS when irradiated with various types of ionizing radiation (photons or protons), the pronounced MRI contrast properties, as well as low cytotoxicity, we can confidently talk about the prospects for their biomedical use as a radiosensitizer in the future.

title: Radiomics-defined prognostic phenotypes are associated with transcriptomic variation and candidate therapeutic vulnerability states in glioblastoma.
abstract: Objective To develop and externally evaluate a radiogenomic framework that links an MRI-derived prognostic phenotype to transcriptomic features, pathway-level heterogeneity, and exploratory therapeutic vulnerability states in glioblastoma. Methods Pretreatment multiregional radiomic features were extracted from T1-weighted, T2-weighted, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI. A hierarchical radiomics survival model was developed using 156 patients from the UCSF-PDGM cohort, internally evaluated in 67 patients, and independently evaluated in 98 TCGA-GBM patients. In the 88 external patients with matched RNA-sequencing data, the continuous radiomics-derived risk phenotype was aligned with transcriptomic profiles. Radiomics-associated genes were characterized, preranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed, and patient-level pathway activity was related to the continuous imaging risk score. Molecular signals were subsequently organized into exploratory therapeutic vulnerability states and pathway-aligned treatment hypotheses. title: Automated tool support for brain tumor diagnosis with explainability using MRI images.
abstract: Precise and early detection of brain tumors is very important for successful clinical decision making. However the prevailing models didn't perform well on noisy images, also they didn't perform feature extraction to gather relevant tumor information. Most of the existing models produce good detection results with high complex architecture, increasing computational expensive. Moreover, these models have less interpretability and lacking accurate tumor detection, decreasing clinical decision making capability. To solve these issues, lightweight deep learning (DL) models is proposed in this research for accurate tumor segmentation and classification. This system include phase's namely pre-processing, segmentation, feature extraction, classification, model optimization and explainability. Experimental results are conducted on BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2018 datasets, proposed model produced accuracy of 99.75%, and 99.5% respectively.

title: Prognostic value of right ventricular ejection fraction measured by cardiac magnetic resonance in patients with transthyretin amyloidosis.
abstract: Introduction Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) plays an important role in both the diagnosis and follow-up of patients with transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CM), as it provides information on cardiac function, structure, and tissue characterization. Moreover, it is the gold standard for right ventricular (RV) assessment. However, evidence regarding the prognostic value of RV systolic dysfunction in this population remains limited. Objective To evaluate the prognostic value of right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF) measured by CMR in patients with ATTR-CM. MéTODOS: This was a single-center, observational, retrospective cohort study. We included patients from an institutional ATTR-CM registry who underwent CMR within 6 months of diagnosis between 2011 and 2025. Patients with other types of amyloidosis were excluded. Clinical, biochemical, echocardiographic, and CMR variables were collected. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier curves were constructed according to the presence or absence of RV dysfunction on CMR, defined as RVEF <50%. Univariate and multivariable Cox regression models were performed to identify predictors of the primary endpoint. TAPSE was not included in the multivariable models to avoid collinearity. Resultados A total of 100 patients were included, with a median age of 79 years [IQR 73-84]; 84% were men. Median left ventricular ejection fraction was 50% [IQR 42-62], and median RVEF was 48% [IQR 38-57]. Patients with lower RVEF had higher all-cause mortality (log-rank p = 0.008, Figure). In the multivariable model including age, atrial fibrillation, and NT-proBNP, RVEF was independently associated with all-cause mortality (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-0.98; p = 0.002, Table). Conclusiones In our cohort of patients with ATTR-CM, RVEF assessed by CMR was independently associated with all-cause mortality. These findings suggest that RV assessment may provide additional value for risk stratification in this population.

title: [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose-PET in Therapeutic Decision-Making and Theranostics of Breast Cancer.
abstract: [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-PET/CT informs decisions at almost every point in breast cancer care. It establishes the extent of disease at diagnosis and so determines whether treatment is delivered with curative or palliative intent. This review examines the biology that underlies FDG uptake and explains why uptake varies so markedly between molecular subtypes. It also sets out the evidence supporting FDG-PET/CT in staging and in therapeutic decision-making across chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, HER2-directed treatment, immunotherapy, and radiotherapy planning, before turning to the complimentary role of 18F-FDG PET/CT with theranostic agents.

title: [18F]-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET in Lymphoma: Therapeutic Decision-Making and Theranostic Perspectives.
abstract: [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/computed tomography is central to the management of FDG-avid lymphomas, providing whole-body assessment of viable metabolic disease across staging, treatment planning, and response evaluation. Its clinical value lies not simply in detecting residual metabolic activity, but in interpreting PET findings according to lymphoma subtype, treatment context, and their therapeutic consequences. Emerging quantitative biomarkers, long-axial field-of-view PET, and target-specific tracers may further characterize disease burden, heterogeneity, and therapeutic vulnerability, extending PET beyond conventional metabolic imaging toward more individualized and increasingly theranostic lymphoma management.

title: Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET in Theranostics and Therapeutic Decision-Making of Lung Cancer.
abstract: Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT) is central to lung cancer staging and can alter treatment intent by detecting occult nodal and distant disease. FDG PET/CT contributes to treatment planning, biopsy targeting, radiotherapy delineation and assessment of metabolic response. Quantitative PET parameters provide complementary information on tumor burden, biological aggressiveness, and prognosis. Programmed death-ligand 1, fibroblast activation protein, and somatostatin receptor PET extend molecular imaging toward noninvasive assessment of tumor phenotype and potential theranostic targets. Artificial intelligence and radiomics may characterize tumor heterogeneity and predict molecular phenotype and treatment response but require further standardization and validation.

title: Valuable Role of 18 F-Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET/computed Tomography in Therapeutic Decision-Making of Infectious and Inflammatory Disorders.
abstract: 18F-FDG (18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose)-PET/computed tomography (CT) has emerged as a pivotal molecular imaging modality that extends beyond diagnosis to influence therapeutic decision-making in infectious and inflammatory diseases. By detecting increased glucose metabolism in activated inflammatory cells, it enables whole-body visualization of active disease before structural abnormalities become apparent on conventional imaging. Quantitative parameters support reproducible longitudinal monitoring. Its incorporation into international guidelines highlights its growing role in precision-guided management. Emerging technologies, including digital and long axial field-of-view PET/CT, artificial intelligence, radiomics, PET/MR imaging, and pathogen-specific or immune cell-specific tracers, may further enhance diagnostic accuracy and personalized treatment.

title: Critical Role of Novel PET-Computed Tomography/MR Imaging-Based Quantitative Techniques in Assessing Efficacy of Theranostics.
abstract: Theranostics pairs a molecularly targeted diagnostic imaging agent with its therapeutic counterpart, enabling personalized, molecularly guided therapy. Although 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography is not itself a theranostic radiopharmaceutical, it complements the theranostic workflow from patient selection and treatment planning of primary and metastatic sites to quantitative response assessment. This article reviews novel PET-computed tomography/MR imaging-based quantitative techniques for assessing theranostic efficacy, including volumetric and global disease burden metrics, kinetic modeling, and multimodality integration, with applications in thoracic malignancies, metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, and neuroendocrine tumors.

title: Hypoxia imaging as a radiomics signature in tumors using novel 19 F-Eu-based contrast agents for magnetic resonance imaging.
abstract: Purpose Accurately identifying and characterizing tumor hypoxia is critical for understanding disease biology and treatment response, yet current in vivo methods provide limited direct, spatially resolved information. Taking osteosarcoma as a model, an integrated framework is demonstrated combining a novel hypoxia-responsive magnetic resonance probe with spatial transcriptomics to define hypoxia-mediated biology in osteosarcoma. Methods A newly developed hypoxia-responsive contrast agent, which involves both 19 F and Eu II , was applied to osteosarcoma tumors via convection-enhanced delivery. Hypoxia-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging was performed in vivo, followed by spatial transcriptomic profiling of resected tumors to map hypoxia-associated transcriptional programs at high spatial resolution. Results Convection-enhanced delivery provided reliable and reproducible distribution of the contrast agent throughout osteosarcoma tumors, supporting robust hypoxia imaging. Integration of direct hypoxia MRI with spatial transcriptomics enabled localization of hypoxic regions and identification of hypoxia-associated gene expression signatures and putative biomarkers linked to tumor progression and treatment response. Conclusion This study establishes a generalizable framework that couples direct hypoxia-detecting MRI with spatial biology to define hypoxia-mediated tumor biology in vivo. By moving from indirect surrogate measures to direct hypoxia imaging, our approach has the potential to improve detection, monitoring, and therapeutic stratification for osteosarcoma and other hypoxia-driven diseases.

title: Increased abdominal visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in patients with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma under ALK inhibitors is associated with prolonged progression-free survival.
abstract: Background Weight gain due to adipose tissue increase has been reported in patients with ALK-rearranged NSCLC (ALK-NSCLC) treated with anti-ALK agents. However, whether adipose tissue gain is associated with detrimental or favorable outcomes in these patients is not known. Materials and methods In this single-center retrospective study, we analyzed longitudinal body composition parameters in 51 patients with ALK-NSCLC treated with first- and second-generation anti-ALK agents. Semiautomated quantification of subcutaneous (SAT), visceral (VAT), intramuscular (IMAT), and total adipose tissue (TAT), as well as skeletal muscle tissue (SMT), was performed using routine CT scans at baseline and at 4, 8, and 12 months after treatment initiation. Results An early hypercatabolic phase characterized by adipose and muscle tissue reduction was observed during the first 4 months. At 12 months (predominantly during alectinib treatment), >50% of patients experienced a ≥ 20% increase from baseline in VAT, SAT, and TAT, while 62.5% showed SMT loss. Patients with a VAT increase >10% at 12 months had significantly improved progression-free survival (median PFS not reached vs 27 months; p = .008). In multivariate analysis, VAT increase >10% remained independently associated with reduced risk of disease progression (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.15-0.99; p = 0.048). Conclusion Following an early hypercatabolic phase, progressive adipose tissue gain occurs during anti-ALK therapy. VAT increase at 12 months was independently associated with improved PFS. These findings highlight the clinical relevance of metabolic changes during ALK inhibition and support proactive dietary and physical activity counseling to counteract the long-term consequences of sarcopenic obesity in this setting.

title: Outcome of magnetic resonance guided stereotactic body radiotherapy for hepatocellular carcinoma - an R-IDEAL stage IIb trial.
abstract: Introduction Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is gaining increasing importance as a non-invasive, ablative treatment. However, there are still limited data on online magnetic resonance imaging-guided SBRT (MRgSBRT) for HCCs using MR linear accelerators. The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and oncological outcomes of online adaptive MRgSBRT in patients with HCC. Material and methods All patients who underwent liver MR-guided SBRT for HCC using fraction doses of at least 5 Gy between August 2019 and September 2024 were included. All patients were treated on a 1.5 T magnetic resonance (MR-)-Linac with MR imaging for online adaptation and motion monitoring at each fraction. Treatment-related parameters, local control (LC), overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) are reported. Results A total of 45 patients with 51 lesions were treated with online adaptive MRgSBRT. Median age was 72 (interquartile range, IQR 67 to 78) years. Liver-directed treatments prior to the SBRT had been applied in 53% of patients. A median of 35 (IQR of 35 to 40) Gray (Gy) was applied with a median of 5 fractions. Median follow-up was 28 months (95% confidence interval, CI: 21-35). LC at 12 and 24 months was 94% (95% CI: 86-100) and 90% (95% CI 79-100). OS after 12 and 24 months were 84% (95% CI: 73-96) and 70% (95% CI: 56-87) and PFS was 54.7% (95% CI: 41-74) and 29% (95% CI: 17%-50%). Of the 14 patients treated for bridging 8 patients (57%) proceeded to receive liver transplantation. No acute adverse events beyond CTCAE grade 2 were documented. Conclusion Non-invasive, online adaptive MRgSBRT for HCC in this prospective cohort of patients proved to be well tolerated with excellent local control and is therefore a viable treatment option for patients with HCC.

title: Global practice patterns of MR-linac use in head and neck radiotherapy: a survey by the international MR-Linac consortium.
abstract: Background Head-and-neck (HN) cancers remain prevalent, and most patients require radiotherapy as part of their treatment. Anatomical changes during treatment can alter dose distribution, potentially impacting both tumor control and toxicity. Magnetic resonance-guided linear accelerators (MR-Linacs) enable adaptive radiotherapy by integrating high-resolution soft-tissue imaging with on-table plan adaptation. However, global practice patterns, expert priorities, and barriers to implementation of this emerging technology remain incompletely characterized. We therefore conducted a survey to evaluate perceived benefits and barriers to MR-guided radiotherapy in head-and-neck cancers. Methods A cross-sectional survey was distributed to experts within the Head and Neck MR-Linac Consortium, assessing five domains: current clinical use, treatment delivery approaches, automation, re-irradiation practices, and clinical trial priorities. Results Thirty-six experts from four continents responded (67%, n = 24/36 from academic centers). Although 86% ( n = 31/36) reported access to MR-Linac technology, only 28% ( n = 10/36) treated HN patients, with a median of 2.5 patients treated per respondent (IQR 1-20). Adaptive strategies varied, including adapt-to-position (40%, n = 4/10), online adapt-to-shape (40%, n = 4/10), and offline adapt-to-shape (20%, n = 2/10). Reported barriers included prolonged treatment times, limited staffing resources, and suboptimal plan quality. Key priorities for improvement included volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) implementation, faster dose delivery, AI-assisted auto-contouring, and standardized quality assurance workflows. Functional imaging, particularly diffusion-weighted imaging, and dose accumulation reporting were also highly valued. For future clinical trials, early identification of responders was considered essential, weekly adapt-to-shape workflows were deemed feasible, and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) was preferred for re-irradiation. Cost-effectiveness analyses were consistently highlighted as important. Conclusions This international survey of MR-Linac practice in head-and-neck cancer demonstrates substantial interest in the technology but limited clinical uptake, largely due to workflow inefficiencies and heterogeneous adaptive strategies. Advances in treatment delivery efficiency, AI-driven automation, standardized quality assurance, and dose accumulation methodologies will be essential to support broader clinical integration and to guide future trial design .

title: Clinical practice patterns for radiotherapy in older patients with head and neck cancer: Results of the ESTRO head and neck focus group patterns-of-care survey.
abstract: Introduction Demographic projections predict a steadily growing number of older patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). As they remain underrepresented in clinical trials, substantial uncertainty persists in their radiotherapeutic management. We aimed to map current international practice and identify areas of heterogeneity that warrant evidence-generating efforts and consensus development. Methods On behalf of the Head and Neck Focus Group of the European Society for Radiotherapy and Oncology (ESTRO), we conducted an international web-based survey covering 34 questions on pretreatment work-up, treatment parameters and supportive care. The survey was distributed via the ESTRO mailing list and social media between September and December 2025. Results 85 radiation oncologists responded, predominantly from academic institutions. Of those providing geographic origin ( n = 63) 41% are practicing outside Europe. Age thresholds defining older HNSCC patients ranged from 65 to 75 years and were significantly lower among non-European respondents ( p < 0.001), whereas structured comorbidity scoring (32%) and geriatric screening (25%) were applied by a minority. PET/CT was used by 62% of respondents for pretreatment imaging. Bilateral elective nodal irradiation was commonly used in the definitive (86%) but less often in the adjuvant setting (66%). Around half of respondents routinely omitted chemotherapy beyond a self-defined age threshold. Weekly cisplatin was the most frequent regimen for both definitive (60%) and adjuvant (63%) chemoradiation treatments. Hypofractionation was the most frequently reported alternative in case of chemotherapy ineligibility (41%). Conclusion This international survey on the treatment of older patients with HNSCC identifies areas of relative consensus among responding radiation oncologists as well as clinically relevant heterogeneity in age-based chemotherapy decisions, geriatric assessment, postoperative target volumes, and supportive care.

title: Two- versus five-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy for low- and intermediate-risk prostate cancer: feasibility of randomization, clinical tolerance and early oncologic control.
abstract: Two-fraction stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) may reduce treatment burden compared with the standard five-fraction schedule, but prospective randomized data are lacking. We conducted a prospective 1:1 pilot randomized controlled trial (NCT05123391; n = 30; 15 per arm) comparing 26 Gy in two fractions versus 36.25 Gy in five fractions for low- and favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer. Primary outcome was recruitment feasibility (target ≥70%); secondary outcomes included acute and late genitourinary (GU) and gastrointestinal (GI) adverse effects (CTCAE v4.03; RTOG/EORTC late morbidity scale), IPSS, and PSA kinetics. Median follow-up was 31.8 months from end of radiotherapy (range 1.7-43.7 months). Recruitment rate was 69.8% (30/43), meeting the predefined feasibility target (≈70%). No grade ≥ 3 acute events occurred in either arm. Acute GI adverse effects grade ≥ 2 were 19% (five-fraction) versus 8% (two-fraction; p = 0.606); acute GU grade ≥ 2 were comparable (31% vs. 33%; p = 1.000). IPSS returned to near-baseline by 12 weeks in both arms. Late GU grade ≥ 2 were numerically higher in the two-fraction arm (40% vs. 15%; p = 0.341); two grade 3 late GU events occurred in the two-fraction arm (one urinary retention requiring intervention and one bulbar urethral stenosis requiring dilatation). One Phoenix-defined biochemical failure occurred in the two-fraction arm, attributable to pre-treatment understaging, salvaged by radical prostatectomy. Both regimens demonstrated acceptable adverse-effect profiles. These results support a larger randomized trial with late GU adverse effects as the primary endpoint. Pre-treatment multiparametric MRI should be mandatory prior to SBRT. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05123391.

title: Apical extracellular matrix regulates fold morphogenesis in the Drosophila wing disc.
abstract: Tissue folding is a fundamental process in animal organ development. Here, we study the progression of fold shape and the underlying mechanics in the development of the Drosophila wing disc. We present a 3D segmentation of the apical surface of the wing disc proper from larval stages, when folds grow, to early pupariation, when the tissue unfolds and remodels into a bilayer. We establish morphological metrics to quantify and resolve fold shape, introducing a definition of fold depth and width that can be used to characterize folds on a curved surface. Furthermore, we identify fibrous extracellular matrix on the apical side (aECM) that physically connects the two apposing sides of the folds. By modeling a tissue fold with a lateral vertex model endowed with an adhesive layer representing the aECM, we predict that unfolding in the wing disc is preceded by the removal of aECM. Using genetic perturbations, we confirm that aECM affects fold stability and wing disc mechanics: loss of aECM leads to abnormal fold shape and unfolding dynamics, whereas failure to remove aECM at pupariation inhibits unfolding. Finally, we show that these aECM perturbations in larval stages cause morphological phenotypes in the adult wing. In total, our work establishes a key mechanical role for aECM in wing disc morphogenesis and advances our understanding of how epithelial tissue folds can be mechanically stabilized during development.

title: Load-dependent brain network reconfiguration deficits in childhood ADHD revealed by source-space MEG and Graph Transformer modeling.
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is clinically heterogeneous, motivating biomarkers that capture how brain networks reorganize under cognitive demand. We studied 122 children aged 8-12 years (61 with ADHD and 61 controls) during a visually cued attention/inhibition paradigm spanning three operationalized composite demand levels in whole-head MEG; structural MRI supported anatomical source modeling, and 34 children with ADHD completed approximately 6 months of follow-up. After denoising, head-motion compensation, ICA-based artifact removal, dSPM source reconstruction, and Morlet wavelet decomposition, we extracted source time series from 68 DKT cortical regions, quantified dynamic connectivity with PLV, wPLI, AEC, and MI, derived graph-theoretic and hidden Markov model features, and trained a spatiotemporal Graph Transformer. Behavioral group differences increased with cognitive demand, with high-load accuracy showing a large effect size (d=1.71). Relative to controls, children with ADHD showed weaker frontoparietal θ coupling, stronger default-mode α coupling, reduced occupancy of frontoparietal-dominant states, greater default-mode state persistence, lower global efficiency, higher modularity, and smaller gains in network flexibility; frontoparietal flexibility showed the strongest association with inattentive symptoms (r s =-0.78). Under participant-level nested cross-validation, the Graph Transformer achieved 94.3% accuracy for three-class cognitive-demand classification (AUC = 0.981) and 96.7% accuracy for ADHD diagnosis (AUC = 0.991). Secondary presentation analyses reached 83.6% accuracy (95% CI: 73.8%-91.8%), and higher baseline frontoparietal flexibility in the follow-up subset was associated with subsequent medication response (OR = 8.49, 95% CI: 2.31-31.2). In an independent task-matched MEG cohort (n=45), zero-shot ADHD diagnostic accuracy was 90.0% (AUC = 0.952), increasing to 94.2% (AUC = 0.981) after limited classification-head adaptation on a separate subset. Together, these results identify load-dependent network flexibility and state-transition measures as candidate adjunctive biomarkers and define prospective multi-center validation as the next translational test.

title: Brain volumes and their relationship with cerebral microbleeds and cognition in middle-aged adults with type 1 diabetes.
abstract: Aims Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is associated with brain volumetric alterations, cerebral microbleeds (CMBs), and cognitive deficits. We examined brain volumes and their direct and combined associations with CMBs on cognitive performance in T1D. Methods Adults with T1D (n = 163; age 46 ± 8 years; diabetes duration 31 ± 10 years; 53% women) and 48 matched controls underwent brain MRI and clinical and neuropsychological evaluations. Volumetric MRI measures included total brain (TBV) and white matter volume (WMV), and volumes of cortex, thalamus, hippocampus, nucleus accumbens, and choroid plexus. Results Individuals with T1D had smaller TBV, WMV, cortex, thalamus, and nucleus accumbens volumes, and larger choroid plexus, than controls (Cohen's d = 0.39-0.54). Those with T1D and ≥3 CMBs (n = 25) had smaller TBV, WMV, and cortex, thalamus, and nucleus accumbens than those with 0-2 CMBs (n = 138; Cohen's d = 0.54-0.92). Brain volumes were not directly linked to cognition, but CMB burden moderated the associations between TBV, WMV, nucleus accumbens, and choroid plexus and cognitive performance (standardized β: -0.61-(-0.51) and 0.54-0.75, p FDR = 0.006-0.048). Conclusions Middle-aged individuals with T1D showed smaller global and regional brain volumes and larger choroid plexus than healthy controls. Individuals with CMB burden showed associations between brain volumetric alterations and cognitive deficits.

title: Validity assessment of RIDAQUICK helicobacter kits for diagnosis of helicobacter pylori infection.
abstract: Background Helicobacter pylori causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer. Accurate, non-invasive diagnosis is essential, particularly in resource-limited settings. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of the RIDAQUICK stool antigen assay in an Egyptian population. Methods This cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study was conducted at Al-Azhar University Hospital (March 2025-February 2026). Sixty-eight adults with dyspepsia underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Gastric biopsy histopathology served as the reference standard. Fresh stool samples were tested using the RIDAQUICK lateral-flow immunochromatographic assay. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Histopathology confirmed infection in 40 patients (58.8%). Of 35 positive stool tests, 31 were true positives. Sensitivity was 77.5% (95% CI: 61.6-89.2), specificity 85.7% (67.3-96.0), positive predictive value 88.6% (75.5-95.1), negative predictive value 72.7% (59.5-82.9), and accuracy 80.9% (69.5-89.4). Stool antigen results were significantly associated with histopathology (p < 0.01). Logistic regression identified RIDAQUICK positivity as a strong independent predictor of infection (OR = 16.6, p < 0.001). Conclusion RIDAQUICK offers a rapid point-of-care test with favorable specificity and positive predictive value, supporting its use for ruling in active infection. However, moderate sensitivity and negative predictive value limit its use as a standalone screening tool; negative results do not exclude infection when clinical suspicion is high. Limitations include the small sample, single-center design, and reliance on histology as the sole reference method.

title: Foundation-model imaging biomarkers for pancreatic cancer: cross-species discovery of conserved tumour biology in mouse MRI and human CT.
abstract: Background Computed tomography (CT) stages pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) but does not read out the treatment-guiding tumour biology, requiring biopsy. Whether an imaging-biology relationship discovered in preclinical MRI holds independently in human CT is unknown. Methods One pipeline was applied to two PDAC cohorts: longitudinal 9.4 T multi-parametric MRI (169 sessions; 1002 image series, 471 quantitative maps) with terminal histopathology in male C57BL/6 mice bearing orthotopic KPC-derived tumours treated with gemcitabine, a dendritic-cell vaccine, both, or neither, and abdominal CT with matched proteogenomics from CPTAC-PDA. Radiomics and frozen foundation-model embeddings were modelled under grouped cross-validation against five pre-specified paired endpoints, with no cross-species transfer of features, weights, or labels. Findings Applied independently, the pipeline recovered four matched molecular endpoints in both species (CD8 infiltration, stromal collagen, CD8:CD68 immune balance, cytolytic activity), with areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.938-0.960 in mice and 0.780-0.856 in humans. Survival concordance indices were 0.729 and 0.689. After adjustment for age, stage, and grade, the human imaging score remained independently prognostic (hazard ratio 1.87 per SD, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.66; p < 0.001 [Wald test]; combined concordance index 0.726 versus 0.611 for clinical covariates). Findings held in portal-venous-restricted analysis; frozen embeddings outperformed end-to-end fine-tuning in both arms. Interpretation One pipeline recovered matched PDAC biology in mouse MRI and human CT, supporting preclinical imaging to nominate non-invasive CT biomarker candidates for biopsy-sparing PDAC trial stratification, pending prospective external validation. Funding National Cancer Institute; Society of Interventional Radiology Foundation; University of California Irvine Anticancer Challenge Pilot grant.

title: Brain and spinal cord chronic neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis: a large-scale post-mortem study and longitudinal MRI cohort study.
abstract: Background Brain paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs) represent a subset of chronic active, or mixed active/inactive, lesions in multiple sclerosis (MS). Whether chronic neuroinflammation is synchronised across the craniospinal axis and can predict spinal cord degeneration remains unknown. We aimed to evaluate the correlation of pathology, including lesion types and microglial state, between the brain and spinal cord, and to determine if brain PRL count predicts longitudinal spinal cord atrophy. Methods We combined a large-scale neuropathological study with an in vivo longitudinal clinical-MRI study. Brain and spinal cord tissues from 194 MS donors (5317 samples; 8874 lesions) were analysed to correlate lesion types and microglial state across central nervous system regions. For the clinical-MRI cohort, 173 adults with MS [118 women (68%); 48 progressive; median EDSS 1.5] underwent baseline 3T brain and spinal cord MRI, with longitudinal follow-up over a median of 2.5 years. Brain PRLs were identified via susceptibility-sensitive imaging. The spinal cord cross-sectional area (SCCSA) was measured longitudinally at C2-C3, C4-C5, and T4-T9 at two time points. Findings Large-scale post-mortem analysis revealed that intra-donor proportions of mixed active/inactive lesions in the brain were correlated with those in the spinal cord (p = 2.22e-9, r = 0.41). Microglia/macrophage activity scores (p = 4.30e-6, r = 0.32) and microglial nodules (p = 3.55e-4) were similarly synchronised. In vivo, higher baseline brain PRL counts independently predicted accelerated spinal cord atrophy at C2-C3 (β = -0.049 mm 2 /year, p = 0.03), resulting in an ∼9% steeper SCCSA decline per PRL. The association remained significant after adjustment for T2 lesion burden and treatment. Interpretation Neuroinflammation is concordant between the brain and spinal cord. In vivo, brain PRLs correlate with accelerated upper cervical spinal cord atrophy, supporting its potential as an imaging biomarker of progressive spinal cord neurodegeneration. title: Mitral Annular Calcification - Association with Comorbidities and Left Ventricular Mechanics.
abstract: Aims Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is common in the general population, more pronounced in women and patients with left ventricular (LV) pressure overload conditions, which may increase stress on the mitral valve inducing and exacerbating the calcification process. The pathogenesis of MAC is presumed multifactorial but remains poorly understood. Women display a different LV response to pressure overload compared to men, but this association has rather not been thoroughly investigated. Methods and results The DANCAVAS (Danish Cardiovascular Screening) pilot study included randomly selected individuals from the general population aged 60-75 years to undergo a computed tomography (CT)-based screening program. MAC was graded by mitral valve calcification (MVC) score assessed by CT and compared to echocardiographic data. Among 463 participants, MAC was found in 165 (35.6%) with MVC scores ≤100 AU in 20.7%, 100-400 AU in 8.2% and >400 AU in 6.7%. While MAC was most prevalent in men, women presented with higher MVC scores and severe MAC on echocardiography. Patients with MAC were elderly with cardiovascular risk factors. Concentric LV geometry with smaller LV cavities and higher relative wall thickness were highly associated with MAC (p<0.001). From multivariable analyses, relative wall thickness and the mechanical load on the mitral valve (i.e. Stress MV ) strongly associated with MAC (SD-adjusted OR 28.8, 95% CI [15.6;53.5] and 2.97 [2.25;3.91], respectively) and MAC severity (10.9 [7.74;15.5] and 2.98 [2.33;3.82], respectively). The predictive performance was high with AUC of 0.78 [0.74;0.82] by including Stress MV in the model of age, sex and cardiovascular comorbidity (p<0.001). However, relative wall thickness had distinctive importance (AUC 0.96 [0.94;0.98], p<0.001) regardless of sex. Conclusion MAC is common in the general population with the highest prevalence among men. LV geometry and the pressure on the mitral valve are crucial factors in the pathogenesis of MAC, and sex-specific differences in LV response to pressure overload may elucidate why more extensive grades of MAC mainly affect women.
