title: CT-based AI risk support for cystic renal masses: multicenter validation, reader study, and a randomized implementation study.
abstract: Background Cystic renal masses are frequently overtreated. We developed and evaluated the Kidney Imaging-based Triage Engine for Cystic Renal Masses (KITE-CRM), a computed tomography (CT)-based deep-learning pathway using artificial intelligence (AI) to support malignancy risk assessment in cystic renal masses (CRMs). Methods We conducted a multicentre development and validation study in China. In phase 1 (January 2020-December 2021), we developed the system in a retrospective training cohort from a tertiary referral center. CRMs were defined as renal lesions with predominantly cystic features. Corticomedullary-phase contrast-enhanced CT was the sole model input. In phase 2 (January 2022-October 2025), we externally validated the model across five independent hospitals. The core task was lesion-level malignancy discrimination; secondary tasks classified malignant lesions as clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) versus other malignant subtypes and stratified ccRCC as high-grade versus low-grade disease. Retrospective cohorts comprised 3150 patients. The core task used 570 training cases (142 malignant), 235 internal-validation cases (137 malignant), and 528 external cases (160 malignant). Three-dimensional processing used one index lesion per patient and a fixed threshold of 0.586442888. In a randomized crossover multi-reader, multi-case study, six radiologists interpreted 117 external-cohort cases with and without AI; outcomes were area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, reading time, and user acceptance. In phase 3 (November 2025-February 2026), 5869 eligible consecutive adults undergoing contrast-enhanced abdominal CT at Changhai Hospital were randomized 1:1 to AI-assisted (n = 2934) or standard reporting (n = 2935). The primary clinical endpoint was the proportion of pathologically benign lesions among treated lesions. The trial was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500112290); model code is publicly available. Findings Internal-validation AUROC was 0.996 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.990-0.999) and Brier score 0.046 (0.036-0.058). External AUROCs were 0.913-0.999, excluding Test 4 (AUROC 1.000; three malignant cases). External sensitivity ranged from 19/24 (79.2%) to 3/3 (100.0%) and specificity from 100/116 (86.2%) to 33/33 and 115/115 (100.0%). AI assistance increased reader-averaged AUROC from 0.825 to 0.973 (difference, 0.149; 95% CI, 0.091-0.206) and reduced mean interpretation time from 9.7 to 5.5 min. Benign pathology occurred in 28/171 (16.4%) treated lesions with AI versus 104/258 (40.3%) with standard care (difference, -23.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -31.7 to -15.4). The treated AI-evaluable CRM subgroup difference was non-significant (5/29 [17.2%] versus 19/56 [33.9%]; p = 0.105). In post hoc intention-to-treat analysis, benign intervention occurred in 28/2934 (0.95%) versus 104/2935 (3.54%) randomized participants (risk difference, -2.59 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.38 to -1.85; p < 0.0001). Median reporting time was 7.6 versus 18.5 min. Interpretation KITE-CRM improved assisted interpretation and reporting efficiency. Management findings do not establish long-term oncologic safety or CRM-specific clinical superiority. The model complements, rather than replaces, Bosniak assessment, indicated multiphase CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and clinical judgment. Broader prospective evaluation is needed. Funding National Natural Science Foundation of China and Shanghai municipal research programmes.

title: Technical benchmark of a high-speed ring gantry kV-CBCT imager for CBCT-based dose calculation.
abstract: Purpose A CBCT platform (HyperSight (HS)) mounted on an O-ring linac (ETHOS v1.1), is compared with standard CBCT imagers installed on C-arm (TrueBeam v2.7) and O-ring (Halcyon v3.0) linacs, as well as planning CT (pCT). The study focuses on image quality, radiation dose, and dosimetric evaluation (Hounsfield unit (HU) accuracy and dose comparison). Methods Phantom-based comparisons were performed using default CBCT protocols and reconstruction algorithms available (FDK, iCBCT and iCBCT Acuros CTS). Quantitative image quality metrics (noise, CNR, TTF, low contrast resolution) were studied (IQMetrix software). Radiation dose measurements were compared between CBCT platforms and against manufacturer values.pCT-CBCT HU comparisons were performed on HU-density calibration and anthropomorphic phantoms (Mean Error (ME) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE)). Dosimetric evaluations included relative dose deviations (D50%), and 3D gamma analysis. Results The HS imager demonstrated improved image quality and detection efficiency associated with a reduction in radiation doses compared to standard CBCT imagers. HU accuracy improved markedly for HS images reconstructed with iCBCT Acuros CTS yielding MAE(Body) < 29HU except for Head, and |ME (Soft tissue)| <8HU except for Large Pelvis protocol. For density calibration phantom, HU deviations remained within ± 50 HU except for bone densities. Dosimetric comparisons showed dose deviations below 0.5% between pCT and CBCT-based calculations for all protocols using HyperSight with iCBCT Acuros CTS (except for Large Pelvis (0.9%)). Gamma passing rates were consistently above 97.7% for 0.5%/1 mm criteria. Conclusion These results confirm the value of 125 kVp HS images reconstructed with iCBCT Acuros CTS for CBCT-based dose calculation.

title: Multicentre study of activity quantification methods for 99m-Tc-pyrophosphate SPECT/CT in cardiac amyloidosis.
abstract: Objective 99mTc-PYP SPECT/CT imaging is used for diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA). The calculation of quantitative metrics allows assessment of the myocardial amyloid burden and supports therapy response evaluations. This study explores the implementation of reliable metrics and the validation of activity quantification methods in a multicentre study. Methods As part of the IAEA Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy (iTAC) project, a multicentre phantom study was conducted at 10 institutions using 12 hybrid SPECT/CT systems. Standardized acquisitions consistent with clinical protocols were used to compute the activity calibration factors (ACF). Absolute activity verifications were based on cardiac insert measurements with known activity distributions. Multiple reconstruction/quantification approaches (RecMethod) were evaluated, including the institution method (SiteProc) and four alternative ones; results of the computed activity were compared with the true activity meter measurements. Accuracy was assessed using RecMethod-to-True activity ratios, summarized by median, interquartile range (IQR) and coefficient of variation (CV). Results Most institution ACF values (ACF SiteProc ) ranged 75-105 cps/MBq and were consistent with reference CoreLab estimates. Agreement between ACF SiteProc and reference CoreLab values showed a median ratio of 99.6 %, IQR 5.8 %, and CV 9.4 %, indicating no systematic bias. For activity quantification, median RecMethod-to-True ratios were 100.1 % for the SiteProc reconstructions and 97.8 %, 94.1 %, 95.6 % and 96.0 % for the alternatives. Conclusion The evaluated quantification methods demonstrated good median accuracy across institutions providing reliable activity estimates, essential for a robust implementation of quantitative metrics for ATTR-CA. The obtained inter-site variability indicates that precision remains a challenge at the multicentre quantitative imaging studies.

title: An experimental imaging dose estimation method for the phase-II proton CT scanner.
abstract: Purpose Proton computed tomography (pCT) improves range accuracy in proton therapy by directly mapping proton stopping power relative to water (RSP). Imaging dose remains a crucial factor in determining the feasibility of daily image guidance. This study presents an experimental methodology for estimating imaging dose in the phase-II pCT scanner, utilizing phase space data recorded at the front tracker to eliminate phantom-specific corrections. The estimated doses are validated against ionization chamber (IC) measurements. Methods Dose measurements were conducted at multiple locations and angles within two phantoms, with data acquisition triggered by either the front trackers or the energy detector. Baseline scans were also performed without phantoms. Monte Carlo (MC) simulations were used to estimate imaging dose in single projections and full scans. Eight front-tracker-triggered baseline datasets were processed for proton track reconstruction and fluence estimation. After assessing inter-run variability, phase space files were averaged to generate an input source for MC simulations. The simulated imaging doses were renormalized to the averaged datasets and quantitatively compared against IC measurements. Results Analyzed proton track numbers exhibited consistency across datasets, with coefficients of variation below 2.0%. Estimated doses agreed with IC measurements within ±1.8% for the CTDI phantom; head phantom underestimated -4.6% (single projection) and -6.7% (full scan). Uncertainties from multiple measurements remained below 1.9%. Conclusion This study introduces a reliable workflow for imaging dose estimation in the phase-II pCT scanner. The approach demonstrates satisfactory agreement with IC measurements, supporting its feasibility for evaluating imaging dose in image-guided and adaptive proton therapy.

title: Minimum recommended distances between cardiac implantable electronic devices and the applicator surface in low-energy intraoperative radiotherapy of the breast: an in vivo dosimetric study.
abstract: Purpose Clinical guidelines recommend keeping the dose to cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) below 2 Gy. In low-energy intraoperative radiotherapy (IORT) of the breast, the Intrabeam treatment planning system (TPS) estimates dose in water, without accounting for tissue attenuation, reduced scatter at the skin surface and backscatter from tungsten shielding. This study aimed to determine conservative minimum recommended distances between the CIED and the applicator surface based on in vivo dosimetry. Materials and methods Thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs), cross-calibrated against an ionization chamber, were placed on the skin between the applicator and the infraclavicular region, close to the usual CIED location, in 21 patients undergoing breast IORT. Applicator-to-dosimeter distances were measured with intraoperative ultrasound, and dose-distance curves were fitted to identify the distance at which dose falls below 2 Gy (d <2Gy ). Results Tungsten shielding increased the surface dose by approximately 22%, whereas without shielding the surface dose in water was on average 3% lower than predicted under full-scatter conditions. The median d <2Gy exceeded the TPS value by 3.1 mm (interquartile range -1.7 to 4.5 mm), with large inter-patient variability. Minimum recommended distances, defined as the upper 95% confidence limit of the regression of d <2Gy on applicator diameter, ranged from 29 mm (35 mm applicator) to 39 mm (50 mm applicator), compared with 22-24 mm calculated by the TPS. Conclusion Intraoperative ultrasound combined with applicator-specific minimum recommended distances provides a practical tool to guide treatment decisions in patients with CIEDs undergoing low-energy breast IORT.

title: PROton therapy for HPV-related oroPHaryngeal cancer patients using normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) modEl-based strategy: an iTalian multIcenter retrospective Cross-sectional study - PROPHETIC.
abstract: Background Intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) has shown promise in reducing toxicityfor patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), while maintaining comparable tumor control to intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). However, technical, logistical and economic factors have limited widespread implementation. Methods We conducted the first Italian multicenter in-silico comparative study of photon and proton plans in 100 patients with HPV-related OPSCC, involving seven radiation oncology departments. Clinical photon-based plans (mostly using Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT)) were compared with robustly optimized IMPT plans generated using the CNAO beamline. Dosimetric endpoints and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) values for xerostomia and dysphagia were assessed. Eligibility for IMPT was retrospectively estimated using the Dutch model-based selection (MBS)criteria. Results Target coverage was comparable between modalities, although IMPT plans showed slightly lower conformity indices. IMPT significantly reduced the dose bath to healthy tissues, with lower mean doses to the parotids, submandibular glands, pharyngeal constrictors, oral cavity, brainstem, and spinal cord (p < 0.01). NTCP analyses predicted clinically relevant reductions in xerostomia and dysphagia with IMPT. Applying the MBS approach, 36 % of patients were deemed eligible for PT, consistent with previous reports. Inter-center variability in eligibility reflected differences in delineation practices and clinical protocols. Conclusions This study tested the feasibility of a multicenter model-based evaluation for IMPT in Italy. A substantial proportion of OPSCC patients could benefit from IMPT, though results likely represent a conservative estimate due to protocol choices. Standardized delineation, robust optimization, and integration of NTCP models are essential for consistent patient selection.

title: Single prior-based 3D volumetric tracking from a planar snapshot in spine SBRT: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Background Continuous 3D onboard monitoring is essential to ensure accurate dose delivery of stereotactic body radiation therapy. However, current approaches for 2D-to-3D volumetric estimation typically require extensive patient-specific data, or depend on auxiliary imaging hardware. This study introduces a proof-of-concept framework for data-efficient, patient-specific 3D volumetric tracking using only a single volumetric prior. Methods A retrospective dataset of 80 spine SBRT patients was utilized. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs synthesized from cone-beam computed tomography volumes served as surrogates for onboard kV projections. The pipeline consists of patient-agnostic pre-training using an archival dataset, patient-specific adaptation using the single volumetric prior supplemented by non-rigid motion simulations, and simulated intra-fractional 3D estimation. The network employs a modified Attention U-Net with a channel-to-depth bottleneck and a triple feature concatenation to map the 2D to 3D spatial domain. Results The proposed model demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in structural tracking capabilities compared to a static uncompensated baseline. Furthermore, the performance variance across patients was substantially compressed, enhancing reliability against setup uncertainties while achieving high spatial concordance in the complex spinal anatomy. The inference throughput reached approximately 10 frames per second. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study establishes the technical feasibility of data-efficient, patient-specific onboard volumetric tracking using a single volumetric prior by successfully resolving anatomical deformations from a single 2D projection in near real-time.

title: Efficient proton adaptive breast radiotherapy with CBCT-Based synthetic CT.
abstract: Purpose Repeat CTs (reCTs) are routinely used during breast proton radiotherapy to assess anatomical and positioning changes; however, they increase patient dose and workflow burden. This study evaluated CBCT-based synthetic CT imaging for accurately monitoring fractional dose distribution and developed an adaptive workflow for breast proton therapy. Methods A retrospective analysis included 26 breast cancer patients who received both CBCT and reCT on the same day between 2022 and 2024. Two commercial synthetic CT algorithms were studied: corrected CBCT (corrCBCT), which utilizes iterative correction, and virtual CT (vCT), generated by deforming the planning CT to match the CBCT. Treatment plans were recalculated on the corrCBCT and vCT, and compared with same-day reCT metrics. A prospective evaluation of weekly vCT-guided dosimetry was performed in an additional 25 patients to assess its feasibility in adaptive workflows. Results CorrCBCT and vCT produced reliable dosimetric results when compared with reCT. Target coverage, measured by the mean percentage dose difference in D95% to the breast or chest wall, was -0.80% (SD = 1.3) for the corrCBCT and -0.7% (SD = 1.6) for the vCT. vCT also showed good agreement with same-day reCT imaging for dose metrics of adjacent critical structures. Larger discrepancies were observed in nodal targets, primarily due to CBCT image artifacts in the shoulder region. Conclusion Accurate proton-dose calculations require reCT, but synthetic CT can effectively flag tissue alterations. This study shows that monitoring dosimetric shifts from vCT can prompt targeted reCT-based replanning in unilateral breast proton therapy, thereby sparing patients the exposure and logistics of routine reCT during treatment.
originalAbstract:
Purpose

Repeat CTs (reCTs) are routinely used during breast proton radiotherapy to assess anatomical and positioning changes; however, they increase patient dose and workflow burden. This study evaluated CBCT-based synthetic CT imaging for accurately monitoring fractional dose distribution and developed an adaptive workflow for breast proton therapy.

Methods

A retrospective analysis included 26 breast cancer patients who received both CBCT and reCT on the same day between 2022 and 2024. Two commercial synthetic CT algorithms were studied: corrected CBCT (corrCBCT), which utilizes iterative correction, and virtual CT (vCT), generated by deforming the planning CT to match the CBCT. Treatment plans were recalculated on the corrCBCT and vCT, and compared with same-day reCT metrics. A prospective evaluation of weekly vCT-guided dosimetry was performed in an additional 25 patients to assess its feasibility in adaptive workflows.

Results

CorrCBCT and vCT produced reliable dosimetric results when compared with reCT. Target coverage, measured by the mean percentage dose difference in D95% to the breast or chest wall, was -0.80% (SD = 1.3) for the corrCBCT and -0.7% (SD = 1.6) for the vCT. vCT also showed good agreement with same-day reCT imaging for dose metrics of adjacent critical structures. Larger discrepancies were observed in nodal targets, primarily due to CBCT image artifacts in the shoulder region.

Conclusion

Accurate proton-dose calculations require reCT, but synthetic CT can effectively flag tissue alterations. This study shows that monitoring dosimetric shifts from vCT can prompt targeted reCT-based replanning in unilateral breast proton therapy, thereby sparing patients the exposure and logistics of routine reCT during treatment.

title: Visualizing artificial intelligence predictions for clinical experts - Detection of acute rejection from cardiac magnetic resonance images of heart transplant patients.
abstract: Background Most current convolutional neural network (CNN)-based artificial intelligence (AI) models have a limited ability to visualize how the resulting prediction is formed. This overshadows the integration of AI models into the clinical routine. This study aimed to develop a clinician-oriented workflow for visualizing CNN predictions in cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) mapping, using acute heart transplant rejection as a clinical example. Methods We developed a pipeline to visualize image regions contributing to CNN predictions in a clinically interpretable format. As a proof of concept, the workflow was applied to a CNN detecting acute rejection from CMR T1 and T2 maps of heart transplant patients. The model used T1 and T2 maps from basal, mid-ventricular, and apical regions of the left ventricle. The operation of the model was visualized by using class activation mapping (ScoreCAM and GradCAM), and normalized occlusion maps. These methods were applied to input CMR images. The outputs were masked to the myocardium, transformed into a color-coded 16-segment cardiac model, and quantitatively compared with segmental ground-truth findings. Results The pipeline enabled automated analysis of CNN visualization activations and their presentation in a clinically familiar 16-segment model. Substantial intersegment variability was observed. Conclusion We presented a clinician-oriented workflow for visualizing and evaluating CNN predictions in CMR mapping. Using heart transplant rejection as an example, the approach transformed post-hoc AI visualizations into a clinically familiar cardiac segment model. Independent clinical validation isrequiredbefore thevisualizationoutputs can be linked toclinical phenomenaor used in clinical decision-making.

title: CT-ED/MD calibration curve commissioning and end-to-end validation of HyperSight CBCT-Based dose calculation for online adaptive radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose To establish a CT number-to-electron/mass density (CT-ED/MD) calibration curve for the HyperSight cone-beam CT (CBCT) system on the Ethos platform, perform end-to-end dosimetric validation, and evaluate whether a single curve applies across kV imaging energies. Methods An electron density phantom (CIRS 062 M) was scanned at 125 and 140 kV and reconstructed using iterative CBCT (iCBCT) Acuros and metal artifact reduction (MAR) algorithms. A 125-kV curve was generated from the averaged Acuros/MAR HU values. Ten intensity-modulated radiotherapy/volumetric-modulated arc therapy plans spanning five disease sites (glioma, brain stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT), mediastinal tumor, lung stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), and prostate cancer) were created on simulation CT for anthropomorphic head, thorax, and pelvis phantoms and recalculated on HyperSight images using the single curve. Validation included ionization-chamber point-dose measurement, 3D gamma analysis, dose-volume histogram comparison, and equivalence testing. Results The averaged 125-kV curve agreed closely with the Philips 120-kV simulation CT curve. All 50 point-dose comparisons fell within ± 2% (82% within ± 1%), with mean differences of -0.24% to + 0.03% across disease sites, kV energies, and reconstruction algorithms. Mean body gamma pass rates were 99.79% (1%/1 mm) and 99.97% (2%/2 mm); mean target pass rates were 98.04% and 99.79%. Target mean-dose differences versus simulation CT averaged 0.11% (maximum 0.46%), and equivalence was confirmed within ± 2%. Conclusions A single, locally generated 125-kV CT-ED/MD curve based on averaged Acuros/MAR HU values enables clinically acceptable HyperSight-based dose calculation, supporting a simplified single-curve commissioning workflow for online adaptive radiotherapy.

title: Machine log files in modern radiotherapy: a systematic and bibliometric review.
abstract: Background and purpose Machine Log Files (MLF) were initially used to verify dynamic multileaf collimator behavior during early intensity-modulated radiotherapy and are now applied, for example, across machine-performance surveillance and Patient-Specific Quality Assurance (PSQA), yet the literature remains fragmented across application-specific silos. This review aimed to synthesize the field systematically and bibliometrically into a risk-informed QA framework. Materials and methods Web-of-Science Core Collection (WSCC) and PubMed were searched for peer-reviewed English-language articles published between 1997 and March 2026. Screening and eligibility assessment were performed independently by two medical physicists among the authors. A bibliometric analysis (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer) was performed on the WSCC-indexed subset. Results 240 studies were included (224 WSCC-indexed), dominated by Varian platforms (167 articles) but broadened to Elekta systems (46), Magnetic Resonance (MR)-guided radiotherapy (14), and proton/carbon-ion scanning (16). Author-keyword co-occurrence analysis identified five thematic domains: delivery verification and machine performance; PSQA and Artificial Intelligence-assisted verification; dose reconstruction and dosimetric validation; motion-aware and MR-guided applications; and proton therapy and advanced dose calculation. MLF provide high temporal resolution and automation potential but remain vendor-dependent and not fully independent of the treatment-control system. Conclusions We propose a layered, risk-informed QA architecture in which MLF support delivery-integrity auditing, independent 3D dose recalculation, and fraction-level surveillance, while independent machine QA, imaging-based verification, and in vivo dosimetry cover failure modes that MLF cannot detect. Standardised reporting, multicentre validation, and data governance will determine whether MLF evolve into the digital backbone of a predictive, learning QA system.

title: Parameter-guided correction of B<sub>1</sub> inhomogeneity in 3D VFA T<sub>1</sub> mapping: A feasibility study using MRI simulation.
abstract: Background Three-dimensional variable flip angle (VFA) T 1 mapping provides rapid quantitative imaging but is highly sensitive to transmit B 1 inhomogeneity. Although B 1 mapping can reduce this bias, it requires additional scans and is not always feasible in clinical protocols. Purpose To evaluate the feasibility and model sensitivity of a parameter-guided B 1 correction framework for VFA T 1 mapping. Methods Bloch-based simulations generated multi-FA spoiled gradient-echo (SPGR) images in cylindrical and digital brain phantoms. Pseudo-B 1 -related signal nonuniformity was imposed by multiplying a normalized spatial weighting voxelwise after Bloch signal generation. The empirical correction coefficient combined a double-flip-angle (DFA)-inspired signal-ratio term with a predefined Gaussian spatial prior. T 1 was estimated using non-negative linear least-squares fitting. Separately, an in vivo-derived B 1 + pattern was applied to simulated SPGR data, and the parameter-guided correction was evaluated. Results In the cylindrical phantom, corrected in-plane T 1 bias was < 5% under centered conditions and < 7% (TR = 10 ms) or < 3% (TR = 100 ms) at slice edges. Under a shifted-center condition, residual bias reached 119.9%, indicating sensitivity to spatial model mismatch. In the digital brain phantom, local biases after correction were within 5%. Using an in vivo-derived B 1 + pattern, the parameter-guided correction qualitatively reduced T 1 variation compared with no correction. Conclusion These findings support the feasibility of parameter-guided correction under the tested simulations but show dependence on predefined spatial parameters. The framework may avoid a dedicated B 1 -mapping sequence when the required α/2α images are available; however, it does not estimate a subject-specific B 1 + field and requires prospective validation.

title: An accessible efficient intervertebral disc vision-language model training strategy with LLM-based retrieval method for spine MRI report generation.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in healthcare, and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding and integrating information from medical images and clinical text. This study explores a low-cost and effective MLLM-based approach for automated radiology report generation from lumbar spine MRI, aiming to improve reporting efficiency and consistency. Methods To mitigate the challenges of limited data availability and the high costs associated with applying MLLMs to spinal report generation, we proposed using the axial plane of a single lumbar intervertebral disc (IVD) and the adjacent vertebrae as the research subject. We constructed the pipeline of data processing to get disc-corresponding images and medical reports based on large language models (LLMs). Then, We fine-tuned presently mature MLLMs under conditions of 1125 patient samples and hardware limitations, achieving considerable results. Results In addition to performance evaluated using traditional natural language processing metrics, including BLEU (0.24), ROUGE-L (0.53), and CIDEr (1.28), we further validated the proposed strategy on clinical pathological classification tasks, achieving F1 scores of 0.93 for disc pathology, 0.81 for canal stenosis, and 0.91 for dehydrated disc. Notably, the model achieved diagnostic performance comparable to that of experienced radiologists for canal stenosis and dehydrated disc. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed strategy. Furthermore, our experiments show that the LLM-based data evaluation pipeline is stable and reliable. Conclusion This study offers a new perspective on the field of spinal reporting and outperforms existing methods on both performance and cost. Meanwhile, there is a considerable room for improvement in aspects of data volume and training scale.
